10163-mohammedanism-lectures-on-its-orig:
C. Snouck Hurgronje, professor of Arabic at the University of Leiden, gave these lectures in the American Lectures on the History of Religions for 1914 to 1915, published in 1916. His subject is Mohammedanism: its origin, its religious and political growth, and its present state.

The lectures treat points concerning the origin of Islam, its religious development, its political development, and Islam and modern thought. Hurgronje writes as a scholar who knew Muslim societies firsthand. Readers get a clear, early twentieth-century introduction to Islam, from a leading orientalist. The lectures were popular courses, not specialist papers.
10166-what-germany-thinks-or-the-war-as-:
Thomas F. A. Smith, a former English lecturer at Erlangen, published this book in 1915 after twelve years living in Germany. He had already written on the soul of Germany, and here he reports how Germans themselves saw the outbreak of war. His aim is to explain, not to excuse, a view most British readers found strange.

Chapters treat the causes of war, mobilization, the collapse of the Social Democrats, Belgium, atrocity charges, and the literature of hate. Smith quotes German papers, books, and talk to show a nation sure of its own right. Readers get a rare, first-hand guide to wartime German opinion.
10701-the-history-of-rome-book-i-the-per:
Theodor Mommsen opens his History of Rome with Book I, covering the period before the kings were abolished. In William Purdie Dickson's sanctioned translation, revised throughout, Mommsen traces Rome's earliest age: its peoples, its kings, and the growth of the city before the republic began. The book sets out the ground the later volumes build on.

Mommsen writes with legal precision and narrative force, explaining early institutions, tribes, and customs. His notes draw on Latin, Greek, and other ancient tongues. Readers starting the great history here get Rome's origins told by the master who reshaped the field.
10955-the-gospels-in-the-second-century-:
W. Sanday, rector of Barton-on-the-Heath and former fellow of Trinity College, Oxford, wrote this 1876 reply to the anonymous work Supernatural Religion. Published at the cost of the Christian Evidence Society, the book examines quotations from the Gospels in second-century Christian writers, chapter by chapter, from the Apostolic Fathers and Justin Martyr through Marcion.

Sanday tests whether early writers knew the four Gospels, using the Muratorian Fragment and evidence for the Fourth Gospel. The argument is scholarly and detailed, aimed at readers who follow biblical criticism. It remains a source for Victorian debates on the age and authority of the Gospels.
1121-as-you-like-it:
Rosalind is banished from court by her usurping uncle. She flees to the Forest of Arden dressed as a boy, where she meets her love Orlando and teaches him how to woo. Her father and his foes wander the same woods. William Shakespeare's pastoral comedy is his sunniest.

The forest gathers dukes, shepherds, clowns, and the melancholy Jaques, whose "All the world's a stage" speech crowns the play. Songs, wrestling, and wit carry the lovers to four weddings. The comedy still charms with its warmth, its wordplay, and its green world.
11218-highroads-of-geography-introductor:
The Royal School Series published this 1916 geography primer, Highroads of Geography, Introductory Book: Round the World with Father, illustrated by masterpieces of Turner, Goodall, Hornel, and others. The book follows a father's year told in letters home. Its stops include Paris, Egypt, the Canal, Arabs, India, Burma, Ceylon, China, Japan, Canada, the Red Men, and the Eskimos.

Father kisses the children good-bye, steps into the train, and waves until it is out of sight, leaving even Tom, who thinks himself such a man, in tears. In Ceylon, father rides a rickshaw, a large baby-carriage drawn by a man, past bullock carts carrying tea down to the harbour, and notes men wearing tortoise-shell combs. The primer teaches geography through a family's letters, pictures, and exercises, in the plain language of a school reader.
11310-hindu-tales-from-the-sanskrit:
Translated by S. M. Mitra and adapted by Mrs. Arthur Bell in 1919, this children's book brings nine Hindu tales from Sanskrit sources into English. Stories include the Magic Pitcher, a cat, mouse, lizard, and owl, a royal thief-catcher, magic shoes and staff, a jewelled arrow. a beetle and a silken thread, a crow and his three friends, a clever thief, and a hermit's daughter. Questions after each tale invite children to judge the characters.

The introductory note explains that many tales reached Mitra orally, passed down for centuries before being written, and were used in India to train children's minds. The collection stresses self-realization and ethical judgment. For young readers, it offers unfamiliar stories with familiar morals; for adults, a window into how Indian tales traveled west.
11555-our-farm-of-four-acres-and-the-mon:
Miss Coulton tells, from the twelfth London edition with an introduction by Peter B. Mead, how a small household made money from four acres. The preface answers critics, even the charge that she failed to strap a cow's legs, and notes that gates and hedges raised their own questions.

Chapters move from choosing where to live, through a first cow and a second cow, to pigs, pigeons, and poultry kept for profit. The book is a practical memoir, full of small costs and small gains, and it shows how much work a tiny farm could ask of its keepers.
11757-the-velveteen-rabbit:
Margery Williams wrote The Velveteen Rabbit, or How Toys Become Real, with pictures by William Nicholson. The rabbit begins splendid: fat and bunchy, spotted brown and white, with real thread whiskers and ears lined in pink sateen.

On Christmas morning he sits wedged in the top of the boy's stocking, holly between his paws, best among nuts, oranges, a toy engine, and a clockwork mouse. Later he meets wild rabbits, who laugh at his missing hind legs, though he insists he is sitting on them. The tale follows a toy who longs to be real, through nursery, garden, and a fairy's gift at last.
11966-the-village-sunday-school-with-bri:
John C. Symons's Village Sunday-School, revised by Daniel P. Kidder and published in New York in 1850 for the Methodist Episcopal Sunday-School Union, tells the story of a village school and three of its scholars, James, Thomas, and George. Symons disclaims any pretension to authorship, presenting the sketches as plain, useful testimony.

The book's theme is patience in teaching: instruction given on the Sabbath may lie dormant for years, yet not be annihilated, and may bear fruit long after. Episodes show brothers urged by their parents toward union with God's people, and the writer returns often to the text about casting bread upon the waters and finding it after many days.
1219-an-essay-on-comedy-and-the-uses-of-:
George Meredith, the Victorian novelist, argues in this lecture that true comedy is the test of a civilized mind: it laughs at folly without cruelty and teaches societies to know themselves. He praises Molière and contrasts English humor with the French comic spirit.

Meredith's prose is dense and aphoristic, packed with maxims on laughter, manners, and sense. The essay shaped later thought on comedy and the novel. It draws readers who like criticism that thinks hard, and it pairs well with his own comic novels. The essay pairs well with Meredith's own comic novels.
12252-the-prose-works-of-jonathan-swift-:
Temple Scott edited this third volume of Jonathan Swift prose works for Bohn Standard Library in 1898, with a biographical introduction by W. E. H. Lecky. Swift, dean of St. Patrick Dublin, was the great satirist of early eighteenth-century England and Ireland.

The volume gathers Swift writings on religion and the church, the first of two such volumes. Sermons, tracts, and arguments on doctrine, church power, and dissent show Swift the churchman behind Gulliver Travels. The preface sets his thought against the religious inquiry of the eighteenth century. For readers who know only the satires, the volume reveals a serious Anglican mind, witty even in defense of orthodoxy.
12648-the-beautiful-necessity-seven-essa:
Claude Bragdon's Beautiful Necessity, seven essays on theosophy and architecture, published in Rochester in April 1922, opens with Emerson's line: let us build altars to the beautiful necessity. Bragdon, author of Architecture and Democracy and A Primer of Higher Space, argues that the theosophic idea, like a code key, clears up every field of knowledge and human work.

Essays run from the art of building and unity and polarity through changeless change, the bodily temple, latent geometry, arithmetic of beauty and frozen music, to a conclusion. Bragdon joins mysticism, geometry and building, seeking spiritual law in form. The book offers his credo, poetic, earnest and fond of pattern.
12746-the-prose-works-of-jonathan-swift-:
Volume four of Swift's prose works, Bohn's Standard Library, edited by Temple Scott with a biographical introduction by Lecky, published in 1898, gathers Swift's writings on religion and the church, second part. Contents list tracts on the sacramental test. A letter concerning the test, the Presbyterian's plea of merit, narrative of attempts for repeal, queries, advantages and reasons for repeal, and ten reasons for repealing the Test Act are among them.

Sermons follow on mutual subjection, testimony of conscience, the Trinity, brotherly love and difficulties in religion. Scott's edition presents Swift the churchman and satirist, sharp on dissent and establishment. The volume serves students of Swift, Ireland and eighteenth-century religion, in a standard, annotated text.
12767-the-beginnings-of-new-england-or-t:
John Fiske's 1892 history, drawn from lectures given at Washington University in 1887, traces the Puritan founding of New England. It follows the settlers from English persecution to the Massachusetts Bay charter of March 1629, which set up a governor, deputy, and eighteen assistants to rule the company. Civil and religious liberty form the book's central tension.

Fiske shows how a theocracy that sought godly order also planted habits of self-rule, town meeting, and law. The charter's silence on where the company must meet let its government move to America itself. The book remains a clear, lecture-style account of New England's first decades.
12787-an-introductory-course-of-quantita:
Henry P. Talbot's textbook, sixth edition rewritten in 1921, teaches lab tests that weigh and gauge chemicals at M.I.T. Part one covers care, note books, reagents, and gear, while part two works through tests by volume: scales, burettes, stock fluids, and tests for acids and bases. Plain notes guide each step.

Useful cautions fill the notes, from keeping beaker sides cool so oxalic acid does not break down, to guarding iron salts against air. Signs for ions and water use raised and lowered marks in plain text form. The book suits readers keen on old lab craft and on how such tests were taught a century ago.
12909-romance-of-the-rabbit:
Francis Jammes wrote Romance of the Rabbit, translated by Gladys Edgerton in 1920, as a poetic life of a rabbit in the French countryside. The rabbit hears the hunt near Jean de la Fontaine's home, flees over thyme and dew, past blue steeples and valley roads, and stops at a signboard before a dark, silent moss. Fear sets his eyes at the sides of his head.

Later the book turns to Francis seeking God, who receives him in a humble garden where love alone makes beauty, with lilacs, mosses, and a dreaming blue leek. Jammes blends nature poetry with gentle faith. The book charms readers who like animals, fields, and quiet wonder.
12924-the-world-s-best-poetry-volume-08-:
Volume eight of The World's Best Poetry, edited by Bliss Carman in 1904, gathers verse of national spirit, with a study of poetry by Francis Hovey Stoddard. Stoddard, quoting Bacon, argues that studies teach not their own use, but that a wisdom won by observation lies beyond them. Wise readers, he says, use books without worshipping them.

Poems follow in patriotic vein, from Campbell's lines on fallen Sarmatia and Kosciusko to the Marseillaise calling sons of freedom to glory. The mix of study and song suits the series' aim. The volume offers a period anthology of verse that rallied nations.
12942-the-highland-fling-and-how-to-teac:
Professor Grant's Highland Fling and How to Teach It, published in Buffalo in November 1892, is a short dance manual, book number two from the Electric City Press. Grant teaches by exercises built from the dance's own movements, noting that hopping steps must observe the laws of opposition with hands and arms. Letters R and L mark right and left feet.

Exercise one hops four times on each foot, turning fully round, while later parts move through second positions, front and back placements, and turning sections in eight parts. The manual is practical and plain, aimed at teachers and pupils. It preserves a Victorian Scottish dance in step-by-step form.
13072-common-sense-how-to-exercise-it:
Issued in 1916 as part of the Mental Efficiency Series, this manual presents the teaching of Yoritomo-Tashi, annotated by B. Dangennes and translated by Mme. Leon J. Berthelot de la Boilevebib. It treats common sense as sound judgment free from bias, a gift that is common in name but rare in use. Short chapters lead the reader from attention and memory toward clear choice.

The author uses homely cases, such as judging gilt, cloth, and paint on entering a room, to show how deduction should rest on facts already seen. Thought groups, he says, form around one central idea, and calm review corrects first impressions. The aim is practical: to train the mind to pause, compare, and decide, rather than to rush after feeling or fashion.
13136-the-silence-what-it-is-and-how-to-:
David V. Bush's booklet, one of six twenty-five-cent booklets on applied psychology, teaches the use of silent meditation. Bush, author of books on will power and the master mind, promises that quiet thought can bring prosperity, health, and peace. His pages give short thoughts to hold in the silence for grief, failure, and loss.

One thought runs, in full, All is Good, and Bush claims that in spirit there is no wrong or sorrow, only perfection not yet seen. He warns that selfish aims blunt the law, and that riches gained should pass on to others. The booklet is a plain sample of early self-help mysticism, sold cheap and meant to be used daily.
13484-essay-upon-wit:
Sir Richard Blackmore's Essay upon Wit of 1716, reprinted by the Augustan Reprint Society with Joseph Addison's Freeholder No. 45 and an introduction by Richard C. Boys, asks what wit is and when it wounds. Blackmore warns against scoffers who season raillery with sharp ingredients that wound religion and its sincere professors, making them the entertainment of company.

Addison praises a regular, beautiful comedy, chaste and inoffensive to modest hearers, as pleasing, diverting, and instructive. Few such comedies appear, he argues, not for want of genius but because comic poets often live loosely. The volume gives readers two Augustan voices on laughter, manners, and the proper bounds of jest.
13987-speech-of-john-hossack-convicted-o:
John Hossack, a Scots-born resident of Ottawa, Illinois, gave this speech after conviction under the Fugitive Slave Law. He and Joseph Stout had aided the rescue of a fugitive slave from a deputy marshal on October 20, 1859. Judge Drummond fined each man one hundred dollars and jailed them ten days. The American Anti-Slavery Society published the speech in 1860.

Hossack argues that government ordained to secure justice cannot justly serve as a tool for slave catchers. He reads the Constitution as a plain man reads language, not as lawyers twist it. His speech blends moral indignation with legal argument. It stands as a vivid abolitionist document. Readers of Civil War history will find it direct and moving.
14002-cosmic-consciousness-the-man-god-w:
Ali Nomad put out Cosmic Consciousness, subtitled The Man-God Whom We Await, in 1915. Its chapters deal with the new birth, with cases told at length, and with the riddle of a perfect man. Nomad sets the faiths and thought of East and West side by side, and asks if hope of such a man rests on real past events. Buddha's deep yearnings and the maxims of Brother Lawrence follow.

Nomad writes of sight of the soul in art, of signs of deep mind, and of marks seen in those bound for a higher state. William Sharp and Fiona Macleod appear as a case of a twofold mind. Lines from youth show a high state of mind and how it shaped later life. The book blends faith, mind lore, and hope for days to come.
14304-the-tale-of-peter-rabbit:
Beatrix Potter wrote this short tale of Peter Rabbit, printed here in 1916 with pictures by Virginia Hibert. Four little rabbits — Flopsy, Mopsy, Cotton-tail, and Peter — live with their mother in a sand bank under a great fir tree. One morning Mrs. Rabbit warns them not to go into Mr. McGregor's garden. Their father, she says, had an accident there and was put in a pie. The tale is told in plain words for very young children.

Peter disobeys and slips into the garden, where he eats too much and is chased by Mr. McGregor. He runs into a gooseberry net and is caught by the brass buttons on his blue jacket. Friendly sparrows urge him to try again, and he wriggles free, leaving his jacket behind. He hides in a tool shed can full of water, then creeps past a white cat and a hoeing gardener to the gate.
14815-peck-s-compendium-of-fun-comprisin:
George W. Peck, editor of Peck's Sun in Milwaukee, offers the choicest gems of his wit, humour, sarcasm and pathos in this 1886 compendium, illustrated by eminent artists. Short pieces pile up fast: a bald-headed man, a hot box at a picnic, a lively train load, a mad minister and a musical critique.

Editors burglarised, boys and circuses, camp meetings in the dark of the moon, church keno, coloured concert troupes and dogs and humans follow, each in Peck's plain American voice. The humour is broad, topical and often sentimental, and it captures small-town and newspaper life in the 1880s. Read in short bursts, the volume is a lively museum of Gilded Age jokes.
14838-the-tale-of-peter-rabbit:
Beatrix Potter's 1902 tale, first published by Frederick Warne, introduces four little rabbits: Flopsy, Mopsy, Cotton-tail and Peter, who live with their mother in a sand bank under a big fir tree. One morning old Mrs. Rabbit warns them they may go into fields or down the lane, but not into Mr. McGregor's garden.

Their father had an accident there and was put in a pie by Mrs. McGregor. Mrs. Rabbit goes out with basket and umbrella to buy bread and currant buns, while Flopsy, Mopsy and Cotton-tail, good little bunnies, go down the lane to gather blackberries. Peter, of course, runs straight for the garden. Potter's pictures and plain tale made Peter Rabbit a children's classic.
14899-some-remarks-on-the-tragedy-of-ham:
Anonymous remarks on Shakespeare's Hamlet, attributed to Thomas Hanmer and first published in 1736, appear in an Augustan Reprint Society edition with an introduction by Clarence D. Thorpe. The essay judges Hamlet by the plan its author set, asking whether parts that seem faulty serve the whole design.

Even a part entirely in conformity to the author's plan may still trouble a reader, the writer admits, and the remarks weigh character, plot and language with Augustan care. Priced at seventy-five cents in 1947, the reprint puts an early piece of Shakespeare criticism back before students. It shows how eighteenth-century readers argued about a play we now take as a classic.
14993-rig-veda-americanus-sacred-songs-o:
Daniel G. Brinton edits Rig Veda Americanus, sacred songs of the ancient Mexicans, number eight in the Library of Aboriginal American Literature, with vocabulary and notes. Hymns open the collection: Huitzilopochtli, war song of the Huitznahuac, Tlaloc, the all-mother and the virgin mother.

God of fire, Mixcoatl, god of flowers and goddess of artists follow. God of fishing, Otomi leader, goddess of childbirth and mother of mortals come next, with a hymn sung at a fast every eight years, a night god and a goddess of food. Brinton, with an illustration of Xippe Totec, god of silversmiths, presents Nahuatl poetry in translation. The book remains a key source for ancient Mexican religion.
15063-your-united-states-impressions-of-:
Arnold Bennett, illustrated by Frank Craig, records impressions of a first visit to the United States, published by Harper in October 1912. A frontispiece shows the glory of Fifth Avenue inspiring even those on foot, and contents run from a first night through streets, Capitol and other sites.

Organisations, transit and hotels, sport and theatre, education and art, and citizens follow. Bennett, an English novelist, writes as a curious outsider, noting American energy, scale and manners with admiration and surprise. The book remains a lively travel record of America on the eve of the First World War, seen by a writer who knew how to watch a city.
15065-the-continental-monthly-vol-1-no-4:
The Continental Monthly for April 1862, volume one number four, devoted to literature and national policy, opens with the war between freedom and slavery in Missouri. Its writer admits no man can write history of his own times with fullness and impartiality entitling it to unquestioning credence from posterity.

Men are actors in scenes amid which they live, and if not personally active in public affairs, they have friends who are. That frank admission frames a Civil War monthly: essays, fiction and policy written while the war was still undecided. The issue gives readers a view from inside 1862, partisan, urgent and aware of its own limits as history.
1523-as-you-like-it:
Shakespeare's Forest of Arden comedy follows Rosalind, banished from court, who flees in disguise as the youth Ganymede. Celia and the fool Touchstone, to a wood where her father, the exiled duke, lives among lords turned shepherds. Orlando, a younger brother wronged at home, follows and falls in love.

Through wooing lessons, songs, and a wrestling match, Rosalind tutors Orlando in love while hiding her own heart. Four weddings close the play in the forest's green light. As You Like It is Shakespeare's sunniest comedy, full of wit, music, and the freedom of exile.
15954-mary-jane-her-visit:
A children's book by Clara Ingram Judson, author of Mary Jane, Her Book, and Mary Jane's Kindergarten, issued by Barse and Hopkins in New York and Newark in 1918. Frances White supplied the pictures. A frontispiece catches the porter's cry: Thirty minutes to Glenville! Mary Jane travels to visit, and farm life awaits her.

Mary Jane's arrival, exploring the farm, and the hunt for eggs open the visit. Mysterious bundles add a puzzle to the country fun. Judson writes with warmth for young girls, mixing chores with small adventures. The book delights as a farm-visit tale: a city girl, a country farm, and days full of discovery.
16209-lectures-on-the-english-poets-deli:
William Hazlitt delivered these lectures at the Surrey Institution, published in a second edition in 1819 and proofed here against that text. Eight lectures run from poetry in general through Chaucer and Spenser, Shakespeare and Milton, and Dryden and Pope. Thomson and Cowper, Swift and his circle, and Burns and old ballads follow. The series ends with the living poets of Hazlitt's day. Footnotes run serially through the volume, unlike the original.

Hazlitt opens by calling poetry the natural impression of a strong feeling, a definition that guides his fierce, personal criticism. His judgments are bold, quotable, and often contrarian. Students of English poetry will find a classic of Romantic criticism, still lively two centuries on.
16254-the-fertility-of-the-unfit:
W. A. Chapple, a New Zealand doctor, argues in this Whitcombe and Tombs volume that crime and unfitness are growing faster than the rest of society. A preface by Rutherford Waddell calls the growth of the criminal one of the most ominous clouds on every national horizon. It warns that the unfit may threaten the new civilization as Huns and Vandals threatened the old. Chapple presses for speedy action by sociologists and statesmen.

The book belongs to the eugenics debate of its age, with all its confidence and its harsh labels. Modern readers should read it as history, not as science, noting how fear of numbers shaped policy talk. It serves students of medicine, criminology, and social thought in the early twentieth century.
17003-indiscreet-letters-from-peking-bei:
B. L. Putnam Weale edited these day-by-day notes from an eye witness to the siege and sack of Peking in 1900. Part One warns of the storm: guards arrive, Boxers come, barricades rise, and an ultimatum tips the city into war. Part Two follows the siege itself, with fires, food shortage, shells, sorties, and a growing list of hurt and dead.

Later parts track truce talks, diplomacy, and the slow return of a half-normal life behind legation walls. The notes are frank, close, and often sharp about both sides, and they give names, streets, and small daily facts. For readers of the Boxer rising, this is a vivid firsthand diary of a capital under siege.
17134-taboo-a-legend-retold-from-the-dir:
James Branch Cabell retells a mock-ancient legend in Taboo, a slim 1921 volume in a run of nine hundred numbered copies. A memoir of Saevius Nicanor and long prolegomena frame the tale, in which Horvendile meets fate and custom, a garbage man brings forks, and a legal debate and street talk follow. Notes and a postscript close the jest.

Cabell dedicates the book, with sly thanks, to John S. Sumner of the vice society, a clue to its game: a learned spoof on bans, morals, and high talk. The prose is witty, arch, and full of fake scholarship. Readers who like literary jokes will enjoy its straight-faced fun, while others may find its jest too fine-spun.
17212-michelangelo-a-collection-of-fifte:
Estelle M. Hurll's 1900 Riverside Art volume gathers fifteen pictures and a portrait of Michelangelo, with introduction and interpretation. A portrait attributed to Bugiardini fronts the book, and plates follow: Madonna and Child, David, Cupid, Moses, Pieta, Creation of Man, Jeremiah, Daniel, sibyls, Medici tombs, and Last Judgment figures. Most pictures come from Alinari photographs.

Hurll adds a life outline, a directory of works, collateral readings, and a pronouncing vocabulary for students. Her notes stress Michelangelo's austere, masculine temper and his love of strong form. Art lovers will find a handsome, plain guide to the master's chief works, made for study and for looking long.
17276-the-story-of-a-candy-rabbit:
Laura Lee Hope's 1920 Story of a Candy Rabbit, one of her Make Believe Stories, opens with the rabbit rubbing his pink glass eyes three times. Beside him sits a large egg with a little glass window. Chapters follow his new home, a bad cat, a ride up in the air, an organ grinder, a peddler's basket, a bathtub, a wheelbarrow, a party, and a boy's pocket.

Hope writes in simple, gentle prose for small children, with pictures by Harry L. Smith. The rabbit's wonder at each new place drives the tale. Families who love toy stories will enjoy a sweet, old-style picture book of a candy toy come to life, best read aloud at bedtime.
17314-five-children-and-it:
E. Nesbit's 1905 classic, first seen in part in the Strand as The Psammead, follows five children who find a strange sand fairy in a gravel pit. Wishes bring golden guineas, wings, a castle with no dinner, a siege, grown-up size, and a last wish, each with a comic catch. Cyril, Anthea, and their siblings learn that wishes granted to the letter rarely grant what was wanted.

Nesbit writes with warmth, wit, and a keen sense of child logic, and her Psammead is grumpy, ancient, and lovable. The book set the pattern for modern children's fantasy. Young readers will love its wishes gone wrong, and adults will enjoy its humor about wanting too much, too fast.
17633-saratoga-and-how-to-see-it:
R. F. Dearborn wrote this guide to Saratoga and how to see it, published in 1872. The guide leads visitors to the springs and sights of the famous watering place, with period advertisements bound in. One advertisement praises Drs. Strongs' Remedial Institute, on Circular between Spring and Philadelphia streets, as unsurpassed for beauty of location and access to the principal springs.

That institute, established in 1855 for lung, female, and various chronic diseases, had doubled in size during the fall and winter to meet demand. Readers get a practical 1872 visitor's guide, with the ads as part of the picture. The book suits readers of Saratoga, of spa history, and of Victorian travel.
18050-the-house-fly-and-how-to-suppress-:
L. O. Howard and F. C. Bishopp wrote The House Fly and How to Suppress It as Farmers' Bulletin number 1408, issued in 1925 and revised in 1926. Howard led the Bureau of Entomology, and Bishopp served as entomologist, so the bulletin speaks with federal authority.

The text warns that flies mark filth, breed in waste, and may carry germs to food. It then gives plain cures: screens, papers, poisons, traps, and, most of all, clean stables, tight manure pits, and swift removal of waste. It is a short, useful health pamphlet, and a neat relic of the age when the farm bulletin taught a nation to fight germs.
18648-bumper-the-white-rabbit:
George Ethelbert Walsh wrote this children's book for the Twilight Animal Series, published at Chicago in 1922 with color pictures by Edwin John Prittie. It holds sixteen short stories about Bumper, a white rabbit. They run from where he came from and why he was left at home to his sale, a dreadful house, a red-headed girl, and a sewer rat. Later tales bring bats, a raft escape, a fox, a bear, and country cousins.

The book closes with Bumper crowned white king of the rabbits. Walsh writes in a gentle, simple style meant for children aged four to ten. Young animal lovers will find Bumper brave, kind, and easy to follow from tale to tale.
18848-the-continental-monthly-vol-5-no-3:
The March 1864 number of the Continental Monthly, a magazine of literature and national policy, leads with the third letter of Hon. Robert J. Walker on American finances and resources. Writing from London in December 1863, Walker answers the fear that the rebellion must ruin the nation's wealth.

Walker grants that wars waste property and draw labor from industry, but holds that slavery, the sole cause of the rebellion, will end with reunion, and free labor will repay the losses. From the census of 1860 he shows free states producing more than double per head what slave states produce, starting with Maryland against Massachusetts. The letter makes an economic case for emancipation as national gain.
19099-the-continental-monthly-vol-iii-no:
This May 1863 issue of The Continental Monthly is devoted to literature and national policy. It opens with a defence of Illinois, the great prairie state, against recent shame brought by some of her sons, and praises her loyal heart, courage, and high feeling. The Civil War frames nearly every piece.

Later pages turn to patriotism, party strife, and Governor Yates's message, with sharp words for those who put party gain above country. Poems and essays sit beside political argument. Readers get a wartime magazine of the North, earnest, literary, and fierce in its Union faith.
19371-the-forfeit:
Ridgwell Cullum wrote this western ranch novel, brought out by a New York house in the late nineteen teens. The story opens at Rainbow Hill Valley, where ranchmen Bud and Jeff reckon accounts and face raiders, hangings, and outland justice. Chapters follow cattle trails, polo races, and a long-delayed homecoming.

At the center are two women, Nan and Elvine, whose hopes and fears shape the men's choices as much as any raid. Cullum's West is rough and sentimental by turns, with loyalty and revenge driving the plot to a final round-up. It is a sturdy example of the ranch romance of its day.
19857-the-great-war-as-i-saw-it:
Canon F. G. Scott, a Canadian chaplain, wrote The Great War As I Saw It. Its verse salutes England of fathers and sons alike. A mother's voice called men oversea, the poem says. The blood she gave is the blood they spill for her. Scott served at the front with Canadian troops. His memoir mixes such verse with front-line witness.

Chaplains buried the dead and comforted the living daily. Scott's view runs from billets to dressing stations. He writes as pastor first and soldier second. Canadian readers took the book to their hearts. It stands among the best-known Canadian war memoirs. Its faith and grief are inseparable throughout.
20005-a-narrative-of-the-life-of-rev-noa:
Noah Davis wrote his own life in this narrative, published in 1859. He was born enslaved in Madison County, Virginia, in March 1804. His father John Davis and family belonged to Robert Patten. Patten was a wealthy merchant residing in Fredericksburg. Davis learned the saddler's trade and found faith young. His narrative tells how he bought freedom for himself and his family, member by member.

Davis became a Baptist minister in Baltimore after freedom. He published the narrative to raise money to free his last children. Few slave narratives show the economics of self-purchase so plainly. Prices, wages, and years of saving fill his account. The book is both memoir and fundraising instrument. Its plain facts carry enormous moral weight.
20111-with-those-who-wait:
With Those Who Wait appeared in 1918, a book of wartime waiting and travel in France. One bright scene recalls a party driving through French villages toward dinner. They stop at The Elephant on the quay for evening papers. Then they pass Essommes, with its fine old church, Bonneil, and Romery.

Such calm scenes sit close to the strain of the First World War. Those who wait at home, or near the front, fill these pages. The book blends travel, grief, and hope in a wartime key. Readers get a sense of France in 1918 beyond the trenches alone.
20494-the-shrieking-pit:
The Shrieking Pit is a detective novel by Arthur Rees, set in a lonely part of Norfolk. A pit in the district gives the book its eerie title. Rees opens with a note to local readers who might think they know the ground.

He states that all the personages are fictitious. The scenes lie in a part of Norfolk that many Norfolk people will readily identify. Norfolk police officials appear in the story, but they too are invented. The warning only sharpens the mystery: a real landscape, a strange pit, and a crime that needs a detective's patience.
20721-a-little-girl-in-old-detroit:
Amanda M. Douglas wrote popular historical novels for young readers, and her 1902 book sets a girl's story in early Detroit. The opening pages linger on wild vines, deep forests, rivers full of fish, and wild birds. That rich natural world frames a frontier town still close to the woods around it.

Readers meet Detroit through a child's eyes, with daily life set against trade, travel, and a growing settlement. Douglas mixes simple history with warm scenes of home and nature. The book shows how American girls' fiction once taught the past through place and family rather than through battles and dates alone.
21266-bird-day-how-to-prepare-for-it:
Charles A. Babcock, superintendent of schools at Oil City, Pennsylvania, started the Bird Day movement. He had noticed children's interest in birds during nature study in the spring of 1894. His 1901 book tells schools how to prepare for a day devoted to birds. The Audubon Society and the Department of Agriculture helped it along.

Chapters cover the movement's history, the value of birds, and the destruction of birds for feathers and sport. Most of the book teaches accurate study of a few common birds, using government illustrations. Babcock believed that once children studied a few birds well, further study would take care of itself.
21451-ben-hadden-or-do-right-whatever-co:
Ben Hadden grows up in an east coast fishing village in W. H. G. Kingston's Ben Hadden, or Do Right Whatever Comes of It. The village crews man the herring boats, among the finest sea boats in England. Ben's father, a godly fisherman, raises him in the same faith.

Hard times strike the family, and Ben is hurt while saving children from a runaway horse. Lieutenant Charlton befriends him and helps his mother, then takes him to sea. Ben hopes to find his lost brother Ned, who has suffered wreck in the Pacific. Faith, rescue, and tales of island missions fill this short Victorian tale.
21462-the-frontier-fort-or-stirring-time:
A Hudson's Bay Company party crosses a wide prairie at the start of W. H. G. Kingston's The Frontier Fort. Mr Burnett, a head clerk in charge, jokes that their trade will die when settlement comes. Flowers, rose bushes, and waving grass cover the Red River country around them.

The tale builds on fort life in the North-West Territory of British America. Ambushes, shootings, and fast rides fill the action, as Kingston promises stirring times. Traders, Indigenous peoples, and rivals meet on ground where law runs thin. For readers of frontier tales, the book gives a Canadian twin to the western stories of the States.
21795-fred-fearnot-s-new-ranch-and-how-h:
Fred Fearnot, boy hero of the Work and Win weekly, turns from Wall Street to ranching in this story by Hal Standish. It first ran in the magazine on July 4, 1919. Fred has just beaten the brokers who tried to crush him, turning from bull to bear at the right moment. Broker Bellamy, his worst enemy, is left nearly ruined.

Bellamy's nephews hire thugs to beat Fred, and the pair flee New York when the plan fails. Fred and his friend Terry then take up the new ranch of the title. The tale mixes market fights with western management. It is pure dime-weekly momentum: a young hero always one bold move ahead of grown villains.
22080-true-stories-of-wonderful-deeds-pi:
True Stories of Wonderful Deeds offers very young readers short tales of brave and famous acts. Each story comes with pictures and simple words. One tells of the Royal Oak in Shropshire, said to descend from the tree that hid an English king. That king was Charles II, who escaped his enemies in the oak after a lost battle.

Other pieces retell escapes, rescues, and acts of loyalty from history. The book belongs to a Victorian class of gift books for good children. Its lessons are plain: courage, kindness, and faithfulness win praise. For adults it now serves as a sample of how history was first fed to the nursery in story form.
22143-the-panama-canal-conflict-between-:
The Panama Canal Conflict Between Great Britain and the United States of America studies a sharp legal quarrel. When the canal neared completion, America planned to refund tolls to her own coastwise ships. Britain protested that the Hay–Pauncefote Treaty promised equal treatment for all nations. This Cambridge study asks whether refunding tolls breaks that promise.

Its table of contents separates refunding from outright exemption, page by page. The argument is dry, close, and legal, built for scholars of international law. The dispute ended when President Wilson asked Congress to repeal the exemption in 1914. The book remains a precise record of how the canal's first great diplomatic fight was argued.
22282-uncle-remus-and-brer-rabbit:
Joel Chandler Harris published Uncle Remus and Brer Rabbit in 1906, late in his famous series. Harris, an Atlanta journalist, had learned the tales from enslaved storytellers in Georgia. Here a man goes out to his truck patch and finds things missing: a cabbage here, a turnip there, and a mess of beans yonder. He looks round and sees Brer Rabbit's tracks, for Brer Rabbit left his shoes at home and came barefooted.

That theft sets the trickster running through the book. Brer Fox, Brer Bear, and the rest pursue him and lose. Harris's dialect is now read with mixed feelings, but the tales themselves descend from African and Cherokee story stock. The 1906 volume keeps Uncle Remus telling to the end.
2244-as-you-like-it:
Rosalind, banished from court with her cousin Celia, flees to the Forest of Arden disguised as a young man. As You Like It gathers exiled dukes, melancholy Jaques, shepherds, and clowns in the woods. Love affairs multiply there, and Rosalind, as Ganymede, coaches her own lover Orlando in the art of wooing. Shakespeare contrasts court corruption with forest freedom.

Songs, wrestling, and witty debate fill the green world before a mass of weddings closes the play. The heroine's intelligence and humor carry the whole piece. For a gentle, romantic Shakespeare, few plays match its charm.
22588-from-lower-deck-to-pulpit:
From Lower Deck to Pulpit is the memoir of the Rev. Henry Cowling, who rose from sailor to preacher. The catalog record gives no year. Cowling's father served in the navy and took a post as a gunnery instructor with the Royal Naval Reserve in the far north while his son was still an infant.

The title states the arc of the life: years before the mast, then a turn toward the ministry. Memoirs of this kind were popular with church readers who prized stories of rough starts and changed lives. Cowling looks back over family memory and sea service as the ground of his later calling. The book offers a plain, personal account of faith, work, and the Victorian navy world that formed him.
22600-how-to-write-clearly-rules-and-exe:
How to Write Clearly is a manual of English composition, giving rules and exercises for students. The catalog record names no author and gives no year. Its first aim is clarity: clear writing, the author argues, is a matter of mechanism and of handling words well, a skill anyone can practice.

Forceful expression stands higher, the book admits, and cannot be reduced to rules alone. Still, the manual builds from the ground up, pairing plain rules with drills. Generations of school and college writers learned this way, one fault at a time. The book now serves two audiences: learners who want the old discipline, and readers curious about how writing was taught before modern style guides.
23160-solomon-s-orbit:
Practical jokers reach the sky in Solomon's Orbit. Practical jokers lost their jobs over tricks played on astronomers, the tale reports. New plates of newfound objects came back anyway. Three little old cars now paraded across the heavens on them, proud as natives of the sky.

Photographic plates, pranksters, and objects that should not be there build this story's teasing mystery. Astronomy in the age of glass plates depended on patience and trust in the darkroom, both of which the jokers exploit. Whether the cars in orbit are hoax or omen is the question the title's Solomon must judge. The piece charms by keeping its feet on the observatory floor while its evidence misbehaves overhead.
23259-home-taxidermy-for-pleasure-and-pr:
Albert B. Farnham's Home Taxidermy for Pleasure and Profit, issued in 1944, is a how-to book for amateurs. Farnham aims it at hunters, trappers, fishers, vacationers, and outdoor people in general. After years of study and practice, he says, he found no book written mainly for those everyday nature lovers.

Yet such readers, he argues, handle more fine animal specimens than everyone else combined. His volume, part of the Pleasure and Profit Library, was made to fill that gap. Readers get plain instruction on preserving and mounting specimens at home, for love of the craft or for office decoration.
2394-the-grand-canyon-of-arizona-how-to-:
George Wharton James offers a practical and enthusiastic guide to the Grand Canyon in this early tourist book. The Grand Canyon of Arizona: How to See It tells visitors where to stand, what trails to take, and how to grasp the canyon's scale, mixing geology with travel advice. James writes as a lover of the place, not a dry manual maker.

The book captures the canyon at the dawn of tourism, when railroads first brought crowds to the rim. Its descriptions still convey the wonder that draws millions today. Travelers and history buffs will enjoy it alike.
24101-egocentric-orbit:
John Cory wrote this science fiction story of a lone spaceman in orbit around Earth. Near the end of his fifteenth pass, Greenland slips by below. The pilot runs routine checks on his capsule and its instruments. They will send stored data to Earth on the next pass over Control. Up and down have lost their old sense, since Earth and stars take turns overhead.

Two men flew before him after three years of hard training, and both came back in a sense that leaves the pilot uneasy. Cory uses the quiet of orbit to ask how a mind holds up alone in space, far from Earth. Readers get a tense, thoughtful tale of solitude, duty, and the strange view from above the world.
24628-the-tale-of-jimmy-rabbit:
Jimmy Rabbit stars in this Sleepy-Time tale by Arthur Scott Bailey, published at New York in 1916 with pictures by Eleanore Fagan. Its chapters follow Jimmy finding a new tail, troublesome Mr. Mink, May baskets, making somebody happy, and a new wheelbarrow, which he trundles home again in a picture.

Later chapters bring a narrow escape, a great race, leap-frog, a tooth puller, a slight dispute, and a rabbits' ball. Bailey's short chapters and gentle humour suit bedtime reading for small children. Young readers get a lively bunny story, full of meadow neighbours and small adventures.
24759-the-kingdom-of-heaven-what-is-it:
Edward Burbidge, rector of Backwell in Somerset, wrote this short study for the Society for Promoting Christian Knowledge. It answers two plain questions: what did Christ teach about his Church, and what do the creed's words about the holy Catholic Church mean? Burbidge holds that the Kingdom of Heaven in the Gospels is the Church on earth, not only a future hope.

He builds his case from the parables of Matthew chapter thirteen and from sayings about binding and loosing given to Peter and the apostles. Notes from noted commentators back each step. The book gives a clear, short statement of a Church view of the kingdom, aimed at ordinary readers rather than scholars.
25091-reflections-on-dr-swift-s-letter-t:
John Oldmixon's Reflections on Dr. Swift's Letter to Harley and Arthur Mainwaring's British Academy, both from 1712, are reprinted together by the Augustan Reprint Society in 1948, with an introduction by Louis A. Landa. The pairing preserves a pamphlet war over Jonathan Swift's proposal to fix and refine the English language.

Swift wanted a small academy to guard English against corruption, as France had done for French. Oldmixon answers him sharply, doubting both the plan and the reformer, while Mainwaring defends the academy idea. The two tracts give modern readers a direct view of Augustan debate about language, politics, and who should rule taste.
25191-the-continental-monthly-vol-3-no-3:
The March 1863 number of the Continental Monthly, devoted to literature and national policy, opens with a long survey of Turkey. Writers trace the Ottoman Empire from Suleyman the Magnificent to the reforming Sultan Selim. Selim proclaimed the rights of subjects over the old rule that subjects existed for the sultan.

The article weighs Turkey's fertile valleys, rivers, and shores against a government long shut in the seraglio, where sultans ruled as state prisoners from cradle to throne. For American readers in the Civil War years, the survey offered a lesson in how empires decline and how reform struggles to take hold.
25395-the-ministry-of-the-spirit:
A. J. Gordon's Ministry of the Spirit, published in Philadelphia in 1894 with an introduction by F. B. Meyer, treats the Holy Spirit's work in Christian life. Gordon, a Baptist minister, addresses inheritors of the Spirit in a book of doctrine and devotion.

Chapters follow the age-mission, advent, and naming of the Spirit. Sanctification, he argues, joins mortification and vivification: the old self deadened, the new self quickened. What was wrought in Christ, put to death in flesh but quickened in spirit, is rewrought in believers. The cross and resurrection thus rule the whole life.
25838-fair-margaret-a-portrait:
F. Marion Crawford, author of Saracinesca and Sant' Ilario, writes Fair Margaret, a portrait, published by Grosset and Dunlap in November 1905 with pictures by Horace T. Carpenter. A handsome chalked hand pressed to lips in a very un-English way fronts the book, and the volume reached a thirty-seventh thousand by 1910.

Mr. Edmund Lushington opens the tale declaring himself a realist, as if that explains everything. Crawford paints Margaret, fair and complex, through society, love, and art, in a portrait novel where realism meets romance and a woman's character, not plot alone, carries the story.
26024-marge-askinforit:
Barry Pain parodies a brilliant lady's autobiography in Marge Askinforit, printed by Duffield in 1921. Pain says the book grew from extracts of an autobiography full of interesting people, with a quality that demanded parody, and he offers his wreath to the flatteries she has already won. Chapters run from the catastrophic family and ebullient youth to Gladstone, Lloyd George, and Dr. Benger Horlick, the soles, misfires, testimonials, and self estimate.

Marge boasts of sitting on the laureate's knees and dancing with the Prince of Wales, and of a Sunday Times scored in literature and sales. She counts few staunch friends, many discarded for weakness, and calls Peter Cochin too cautious for understatement of her effect. A verse to Margot in heaven crowns the joke. Pain's parody is sharp, fond, and very much of its moment.
26043-sam-s-chance-and-how-he-improved-i:
Horatio Alger Jr. tells how Sam improves his chance in Sam's Chance, printed by Hurst. Chapters run from Sam's new clothes and first day in business to finding a room, first lessons, finances, luck, a twenty five dollar reward, and an unexpected obstacle. Restoring a ring, an investment, Henry as merchant, and how Sam succeeded follow, with a savings bank book, a lost place, and Tim unmasked.

Later chapters send Sam to Boston, through a Fall River boat trip, mutual confidences, a missed train, and a college society initiation. Tim, back from Boston, scorns it as half the size of New York, with no Old Bowery and no Tony Pastor's, and no fun at night. Sam's path runs through honest work, thrift, and pluck, Alger's familiar road to a fair start.
26080-skinner-s-dress-suit:
Henry Irving Dodge's comic novel follows Skinner, a clerk who asks for a raise and gets one, then finds his new dress suit running his life. His wife Honey insists on the suit, cost or no cost, and plans the socks and ties to go with it. Once bought, the suit begins to get in its fine work.

Chapters track the suit's operating expenses, Skinner dodging a magnate, tangling with the 'gold bugs,' and fishing with a diplomatic hook until he lands a curmudgeon. Chickens come home to roost before the ostrich feather closes the tale. The joke stays gentle: a modest man's finery lifts him socially, then bills him for the lift.
2629-lectures-on-evolution-essay-3-from-:
Thomas Henry Huxley devotes this essay to lectures on evolution, setting out three hypotheses about the history of nature. We live inside a system of immense diversity, he begins, and forming just conceptions of its past matters deeply to all of us.

Huxley weighs creation, spontaneous generation, and evolution by natural causes, judging each by evidence rather than authority. His lectures made Darwin's ideas plain to Victorian audiences, with wit and patience. The essay still reads as a model of science explained for lay readers, firm without being shrill. Huxley keeps the tone of a public lecture, plain and direct.
2633-hasisadra-s-adventure-essay-7-from-:
Thomas Henry Huxley tells of Hasisadra, a dweller in the Mesopotamian city of Surippak some thousands of years ago. A strange dream warns him that a great flood is coming, and bids him build a ship in time to escape it.

Huxley uses the old flood tale to compare Babylonian legend with the Genesis story, asking what each preserves and what each invents. The essay is a piece of comparative mythology, written with clarity and dry wit. Readers get both a gripping ancient story and a lesson in reading sacred texts beside their neighbors.
27367-the-art-of-stage-dancing-the-story:
Ned Wayburn published this manual of stage-craft in New York in 1925, through his own Ned Wayburn Studios of Stage Dancing, priced at five dollars. Its subtitle calls stage dancing the story of a beautiful and profitable profession, and Wayburn writes for students, teachers, and the public who have sat in front at his productions.

Wayburn refuses to call his opening a preface, since he doubts anyone reads prefaces, and greets his readers directly instead. The book sets out the hard work, thought, and skill behind pleasing stage results, and the methods he taught his many pupils. Dancers and theatre historians will find a firsthand account of Broadway training in the 1920s.
27496-continental-monthly-vol-4-no-3-sep:
The Continental Monthly, devoted to literature and national policy, published this number, volume four, number three, in September 1863, in the middle of the Civil War. Its opening article, Southern Hate of New England, sets the tone: a fair and dispassionate analysis of a bitter sectional feeling, traced to its moral and political causes.

The writer argues that days shaking with political feeling and national war call for a deeper look at moral causes and effects than any drama ever played on the world's stage. The magazine mixes literature with such policy writing throughout. The issue gives a vivid window on Northern thinking in 1863.
28163-the-higher-powers-of-mind-and-spir:
Ralph Waldo Trine wrote The Higher Powers of Mind and Spirit, first published in May 1918, as a sequel in spirit to In Tune with the Infinite. Trine argues that mind, through the subconscious, builds and rebuilds body, and that thought acts as a force in daily living. Chapters treat soul, mind, and body, methods of attainment, and the lessons of the World War.

Trine also reads Jesus as the supreme teacher of inner powers, and closes with peace and the world's balance-wheel. His tone is earnest, hopeful, and plain. The book offers a clear sample of early twentieth-century New Thought writing on health, faith, and the mind.
28465-the-limit:
Ada Leverson's The Limit, originally published in 1911, is a society comedy centred on Valentia Wyburn and her husband Romer. The novel opens with Valentia telling Romer, very prettily and very seriously, that it will look better if he does not come with her to Harry's dinner after all.

Harry de Freyne, Valentia's cousin, painted her portrait, The Gilded Lily, his sole success in art. Chapters follow Valentia, Harry, Van Buren, Daphne, and their circle through fancy dress, engagements, proposals, and a Sunday afternoon in the rose garden. Leverson writes with wit about marriage, manners, and the limits of social charm.
29517-john-and-betty-s-history-visit:
Margaret Williamson's 1910 book, printed in Boston by Lothrop, Lee and Shepard, follows two eager young Americans, John and Betty, on a history visit to England. They land in the morning, take an English train toward London, and sit one on each side of the window, eager for all they will see. Pictures from photographs illustrate their tour.

Chapters take them to Westminster Abbey, Penshurst Place, home of Sir Philip Sidney, the Tower of London, and St. Paul's Cathedral. Windsor Castle, Stoke Poges, and Eton School follow, with a Sunday night chat to sort it all. Young readers and lovers of travel tales will find a bright, instructive tour of historic England.
30241-the-person-and-work-of-the-holy-sp:
R. A. Torrey sets out the person and work of the Holy Spirit as revealed in Scripture and in personal experience. Revell published the volume in 1910, in New York, Chicago, Toronto, London, and Edinburgh. Early chapters treat the personality and deity of the Spirit, the distinction from the Father and from the Son, Jesus Christ, and subordination to Father and Son. Names of the Spirit, work in the material universe, and conviction of the world of sin, righteousness, and judgment follow.

Later chapters cover witness to Jesus Christ, regenerating work, and an indwelling Spirit who fully and forever satisfies. Freedom from indwelling sin, Christ formed within, and Christlike graces of character close the main argument. Guidance into life as a son, witness to sonship, and teaching follow, with prayer, thanks, and worship in the Spirit. Torrey writes as an evangelist for believers who want doctrine joined to experience.
30438-the-eyes-have-it:
James McKimmey sets a science fiction tale on an occupied Mars, where Joseph Heidel leads the Superior Council after four of his six years on the planet. Five top officials, chosen and screened on Earth, form the core of rule there, and Heidel watches them closely over a dinner table thick with cigar smoke.

Daylight hides what darkness shows, and the Martians' glowing eyes point to a secret the rulers have missed. Heidel, near fifty-two yet looking far younger, studies faces, motives, and silences as danger gathers around the table. The story turns on close watchfulness, trust among rulers, and what an alien world reveals only after dark.
30449-the-way-to-god-and-how-to-find-it:
D. L. Moody gathers addresses given in cities in Great Britain and his own country into a small evangelical volume, entered for copyright in 1884. He states his aim plainly: to point out the way to God, drawing on talks that had already been heard from the pulpit and adding new matter for print.

Moody begins with the love of God as the source of gifts of grace, then answers the question of how a person can be just with God. He speaks to representative classes of listeners, meeting special needs with direct, plain language. The book reads as preaching in print, short, urgent, and meant to lead a reader toward faith.
30551-the-humourous-story-of-farmer-bump:
Richard Harris, barrister at law and author of Hints on Advocacy, writes The Humourous Story of Farmer Bumpkin's Lawsuit, in a second edition published in London in 1883 by Stevens and Sons. Harris notes enormous public interest in a faster, more effective system of justice, and says a second edition was called for soon after the first.

Proof of evils in the present system, he argues, lies in Smitherman versus the South Eastern Railway Company, recently before the House of Lords. Bumpkin's lawsuit satirizes courts, lawyers, and delays through a farmer's comic legal ordeal. Harris writes with insider wit, making law both funny and a target for reform.
30668-daisy-s-necklace-and-what-came-of-:
T. B. Aldrich writes Daisy's Necklace, and What Came of It, a literary episode published in New York and Cincinnati in 1857 and entered for copyright in 1856. Dedicated to C. L. F., noble merchant and good friend, the book calls itself a burlesque of things in general, with a Lear epigraph about little dogs barking.

Contents open with a prologue and a chapter on little castle builders, set in a house by the sea with a round window, flowers as God's eyes, and daydreamers on the shore. Shell hunting, Bell's freak, Mortimer's dream, and sleep follow. A second chapter, The Dead Hope, turns to time's changes and fallen castles. Aldrich blends satire, sentiment, and literary play.
30833-the-eyes-have-it:
Randall Garrett wrote this science fiction story, printed in Analog in January 1964, about a history slipped slightly sideways. In its world a single great man acted differently, and magic, was developed, yet the year feels like here and now. Its hero is Sir Pierre Morlaix, Chevalier of the Angevin Empire, Knight of the Golden Leopard, and secretary-in-private to the Count D'Evreux.

Sir Pierre glances at his wrist watch at three minutes to seven, after the Angelus rang at six and woke his lord, as it has for seventeen years. Once a sacristan failed to ring the bell, and only Father Bright's intercession, backed by the bishop, saved him from the dungeons of Castle D'Evreux. Garrett mixes medieval court life with modern habits, in a witty tale of magic, rank, and daily routine.
31516-the-eyes-have-it:
Philip K. Dick's short science-fiction story The Eyes Have It is a comic tale of invasion, told in the first person. The narrator says he discovered, quite by accident, an astonishing invasion of Earth by beings from another planet. The plot turns on a government pamphlet about frame-house repair and upkeep, obtained by writing to the authorities.

The clue came from a paperback book left on a bus. In it, a line read that his eyes slowly roved about the room, and nobody in the story showed surprise. That failure of surprise tipped the narrator off: the eyes, he realized, moved through the air on their own. Dick turns a pulp cliché into a joke about reading literally, and the story's humor grows from that single, startling observation.
31529-modern-marriage-and-how-to-bear-it:
Maud Churton Braby's Modern Marriage and How to Bear It, by the author of Downward, examines marriage as it stood in the early twentieth century. Part one, Signs of Unrest, opens with the mutual dissatisfaction of the sexes. It asks why men do not marry and why women do not marry, and closes with the tragedy of the undesired. Part two, Causes of Failure, takes up the various kinds of marriage and why couples fall out. It also covers the age to marry, wild oats for wives, and a plea for the wiser training of girls.

Part three, Suggested Alternatives, proposes leasehold marriage after Meredith, stages a dialogue set in 1999, and judges the fiasco of free love. Readers will find a lively period document, where Edwardian anxieties about sex, marriage, and freedom are argued in plain, provocative prose.
31587-pursuit:
Lester del Rey's science-fiction story Pursuit, illustrated by Orban, opens with fear cutting through the unconscious mind of Wilbur Hawkes. Hawkes dreams he is a soft egg in a huge globe of trembling jelly, while two creatures swim menacingly toward him through the resisting globe. One draws near and makes a mystic pass, and Hawkes screams at it, until the gelatine grows stronger and throws the creatures back. A door opens, and they are gone, but Hawkes cannot let them go.

For a second, the nightmare holds so strongly that he seems to see two figures beyond the door, hurrying down the steps. Del Rey's story follows Hawkes from dream to waking pursuit, where nightmare and reality blur. Readers will find a tense, psychological science-fiction tale, built on a single, vivid image.
31629-scotland-yard-the-methods-and-orga:
George Dilnot's Scotland Yard, the methods and organisation of the Metropolitan Police, was published in London by Percival Marshall and Company, with copyright in the United States in 1915. It is a study of London's police from inside. Its chapters open with the silent machine, move to matters of organisation and the real detective, and continue through fourteen chapters on how the Yard worked. Dilnot writes for a public fascinated by detectives, offering fact beside fiction.

The book explains the Yard's departments, its men, and its methods, from the beat to the detective branch. Readers will learn how cases were organized, how information moved, and what a detective actually did. For students of policing and of detective fiction, Dilnot's account remains a useful contemporary guide to the world's most famous police force.
3177-roughing-it:
Mark Twain calls this book a personal narrative, not a pretentious history or a philosophical dissertation. It records several years of variegated vagabondizing in the American West. Twain wrote it to help the resting reader while away an idle hour. He would rather amuse than afflict his reader with metaphysics or goad him with science. Information is present, Twain admits, but pleasure comes first.

Stagecoaches, mining camps, and frontier towns fill the pages, with tall tales told as sober fact. The book made the West funny for Eastern readers and made Twain a national voice. It remains the best place to meet his humor at full stretch: exaggeration held in check only by a sharper eye for human folly.
31925-the-london-pulpit:
J. Ewing Ritchie's London Pulpit, in its second edition, revised, corrected, and enlarged, published in London in 1858 by William Tweedie, surveys the religious denominations of London through their preachers. Ritchie, author of The Night Side of London, dedicates the edition to John R. Robinson, under whose editorial sanction its contents first appeared.

Its epigraph, from Carlyle's Latter-Day Pamphlets, contrasts the Christianity of Oliver Cromwell wrestling in grim fight with Satan against that of an eloquent modern preacher denouncing capital punishments on platforms. Readers get a mid-Victorian guide to London's pulpits, lively, opinionated, and full of sermons, sects, and personalities.
32069-letters-from-a-cat-published-by-he:
H. H., author of Nelly's Silver Mine, published this children's book in Boston with Roberts Brothers in 1879, with seventeen drawings by Addie Ledyard. Its title page explains the joke: letters from a cat, for all cats and little children. The introduction admits a doubt: the mistress never caught Pussy writing. The letters always arrived inside letters from mamma or friends.

The printing was bad, the letters were signed with Pussy's name, and mamma looked mysterious when asked. The little girl never doubted that Pussy printed them alone after dark. The letters were written while the child travelled with her father in their own carriage, clothes packed in a little leather valise. Readers get a playful epistolary tale, told as if by a cat, for children who like animals and secrets.
32213-hoiman-and-the-solar-circuit:
Gordon Dewey's short story, printed in If Worlds of Science Fiction in July 1952, is a slangy space tale of money trouble and orbit. The cover line says thieves took Hoiman's cash, costing him much loot, so he seized his gear and fled to high orbit. The story opens on pay day. The narrator signs the back of a check and hands it to Nick, the bartender, asking him to leave something to operate on.

Nick turns the check over and asks whether he is still with the News, the narrator lets it pass. Estimating the pile of tabs Nick pulls from the cash register, he dislikes the figure. He feels like a fighter counting the house. Nick adds them up twice, then pulls bills from the drawer. Thirty skins, he says, for the rent. Readers get a science-fiction tale. Pay day leads to the solar circuit.
32890-home-is-where-you-left-it:
Adam Chase sends Steve Cantwell back to his boyhood village on the second planet of Sirius, in a story from Amazing Stories of February 1957. The village greets him as shells of deserted mud-brick houses under a searing sun. Steve came almost five hundred miles from Oasis City by unicopter, remembering a gentler heat from childhood.

At the well he finds the water poisoned, his lips and mouth numbed by contact with it. The town fled on the spur of the moment, leaving a coffeepot on the stove and last night's dinner on a table. Only a withered old Kumaji remains in the shadow of the community center. Steve and Mary then strike out northward across the sand toward the Kumaji settlement, fearing what they will find there.
33165-coal-and-what-we-get-from-it:
Raphael Meldola's Coal, and What We Get from It, explains coal's hidden wealth to general readers. It is a romance of applied science expanded from notes of a lecture delivered in the theatre of the London Institution on January 20, 1890. Meldola, professor of chemistry at Finsbury Technical College, dedicates the book to William Henry Perkin, founder of the coal-tar color industry. His preface warns it is neither a technical manual nor a history of one industry.

From coal come heat and light, gas, coke, tar, dyes, medicines, and a host of chemicals that colored and cured the Victorian world. Meldola tells that story with a chemist's clarity and a lecturer's enthusiasm, showing how a black rock became the base of modern industry. The book remains a delightful introduction to industrial chemistry, and a reminder of how much of modern life once came, quite literally, out of coal.
33344-narrative-of-mr-john-dodge-during-:
John Dodge's Narrative, reproduced in facsimile from the second edition of 1780, tells of his captivity at Detroit, with an introductory note by Clarence Monroe Burton. The facsimile reprint, limited to sixty-three copies, sixty for sale, was printed at Cedar Rapids in 1909. Burton calls Dodge's story a valuable frontier record of the Revolutionary age.

The narrative suits readers of frontier and captivity literature, offering a first-hand account of Detroit, its peoples, and its wars. Its facsimile form keeps the look of the 1780 original, with old spelling and type. For students of the Old Northwest, it is a rare, valuable source on a life lived at the edge of empire.
33371-raising-p-v-squabs-for-profit:
John S. Trecartin's Raising P. V. Squabs for Profit, from Caldwell, New Jersey, is a manual drawn from his own work building and running the largest successful squab plant in the state. Trecartin tells how his plant marketed squabs for twelve dollars per dozen wholesale, and he details housing, feeding, and marketing for a successful business. His guide is practical, plain, and proud of its results.

The book suits readers of farming and small business history, offering a complete, hands-on account of squab raising as a trade. Its tone is that of a man teaching what he has done, not theorizing. For those curious about odd corners of American agriculture, it is a clear, useful manual, full of figures and working advice.
33399-a-romance-in-transit:
Francis Lynde's Romance in Transit, in a third edition from 1899 with copyright in 1897, is a tale of love on the move. Lynde, author of The King of Arcadia, writes of travelers whose paths cross on trains and in stations, where a chance meeting can turn a journey into a romance. The book's title points to its theme: love found not at home, but in transit.

The novel's charm lies in its brisk, railway-age setting and its light, romantic touch. Its characters, met in motion, must decide quickly what they feel and want. For readers who enjoy Edwardian romance with a modern, traveling flavor, A Romance in Transit offers a bright, well-told tale of hearts on the move.
33913-the-wonderful-visit:
H. G. Wells wrote this fantasy novel, published in London and New York in 1895 in Macmillan's Colonial Library. A strange bird comes down by night, is hunted, and proves to be an angel, taken in by a village vicar. Chapters follow the angel at the vicarage, among the man of science and the curate, and out in the village.

Lady Hammergallow and Mrs. Jehoram give their views, while the angel learns human ways with wonder and pain. Wells uses the visitor to poke at village piety and pride. The novel remains a gentle, sharp fantasy from the author of The Time Machine.
34341-the-japanese-spirit:
The Japanese Spirit, by Okakura-Yoshisaburo, was published in New York in 1905. George Meredith wrote the introduction. The talks were given as lectures at the University of London. Meredith praises earlier books on Japan by Lafcadio Hearn and others. Yet he says a son of the land brings the matter closer. The lectures sum up much that had stayed obscure to Western readers.

Meredith traces Confucian, Laoist, and Shinto teaching in the lectures. He notes the part played by Buddhism as well. Bushido, the way of the samurai, stands at the center of his praise. He cites the samurai's readiness to give up privilege for the common good. Feats at Port Arthur and in Manchuria are held up as proof of that spirit.
34861-the-pursuit:
The Pursuit is an adventure novel by Frank Savile, published by Little, Brown of Boston in 1910. Herman Pfeifer drew the illustrations. Savile had earlier written Beyond the Great South Wall. The contents promise a chase across the Mediterranean world.

The lady of the pier and the tent club open the sequence of chapters. A shadow of a name and a character called Despard follow in turn. Landon takes a new profession, and a Villa Eulalia shelters the middle action. The first trick is lost, and an ambush and a trap come after. At Melilla the scene shifts to the Moroccan coast in earnest. The opening finds John Aylmer halted in a Tangier street, staring.
34979-twentieth-century-socialism-what-i:
Edmond Kelly wrote Twentieth Century Socialism, for Longmans in 1910. Its subtitle asks what socialism is not, what it is, and how it may come. Kelly had lectured on municipal government at Columbia University. Three printings ran between May 1910 and May 1911 at New York. London, Bombay, and Calcutta shared the edition with New York.

No one with his wits in working order believes a common claim, he opens. The industrial world is the ground of that opening argument. People are disturbed when one suggests a plain conclusion to them. Industry can no longer be individual, the suggestion runs. Neither should it be owned as men now own it, he adds. Government or Human Evolution and Evolution and Effort stand as his earlier books. Kelly writes as a lecturer turned reformer. The book gives socialism a hearing in plain American terms.
35032-success-and-how-he-won-it:
Success, and How He Won It reached English readers in eighteen ninety-two from Richard Bentley and Son in London, translated by Christina Tyrrell from the German of the novelist Werner. The first chapter opens inside the principal church of a capital. Long lines of handsome carriages wait outside, the altar is rich with flowers, and the pews stay densely filled for a wedding the whole city watches.

A whispering crowd studies the vestry doors until the organ peals and the party appears. First comes a tall, stately officer whose uniform and many orders witness a long career in the service. His simple, grave bearing suits the solemn place, yet something behind the gravity hints at the story to come.
35427-the-raid-of-john-brown-at-harper-s:
Samuel Vanderlip Leech, a minister, wrote a first hand account of John Brown's raid on Harper's Ferry, issued by his own hand in Washington in 1909. A portrait of Brown fronts the book. Leech had written on preaching and on travel, but this small work rests on what he saw with his own eyes.

He opens with the place itself: a town set where the Potomac and the Shenandoah meet, under the Maryland Heights and the Blue Ridge. Few spots in America, he says, match its wild grandeur. From that stage he tells how Brown's band seized the armory town in 1859, and how the raid struck the folk who lived through those days. A letter not bound in the first form is added at the end.
35683-association-football-and-how-to-pl:
Association Football and How to Play It is an instruction book by John Cameron, published in London by Health and Strength at one shilling net. Cameron had played for Queen's Park and Everton. He was player manager of Tottenham Hotspur when he wrote it. His portrait serves as frontispiece.

The chapters teach the game position by position. Goalkeeping comes first, then full back play and the middle line. Forward play, training, and hints to juniors follow. Captaincy and refereeing earn their own chapters. Football as a profession and continental football bring the book to its own day. Famous cup ties close the teaching, and the laws of the game are printed at the end. Photographs show a high save, heading the ball, and centres from both wings. Cameron writes as a working professional for boys who dreamed of his trade.
36055-the-impending-crisis-of-the-south-:
The Impending Crisis of the South: How to Meet It is a famous polemic by Hinton Rowan Helper. Burdick of New York published it in 1859; this copy is the fourteenth thousand. Helper, a North Carolinian, dedicates the book to the non-slaveholding whites of the South. Three named men who had left the South head the dedication list. His preface denies that narrow doctrines moved him to write.

Helper states his subject is chiefly economic. He claims no purpose of casting unmerited blame on slaveholders. Nor does he profess special sympathy for the black population, he says. His case concerns slavery's effects on the whites who held no slaves. Those readers, at home or abroad, are his true audience. The book became one of the most fought over volumes of its decade. Helper sues, in his motto, for simple justice.
36159-the-letter-of-credit:
Susan Warner wrote The Letter of Credit, shown here in an 1882 edition of an 1881 tale. Front pages list Warner's books with prices and praise from the press. The End of a Coil and My Desire stand at one dollar seventy five each. Pine Needles, The Old Helmet, and Melbourne House fill the list. The King's People runs to five volumes at seven dollars.

Review lines call Warner's tales pure and beautiful pictures. They are bright and warm with true love and true religion, one says. A Philadelphia paper praises her vivid New England village life. Her village folk walk and talk in fresh, clear cut form, it says. Humor, a keen sense of the ridiculous, and homely truths in homely phrases mark her hand. Anna Warner's books are listed below her sister's in the same pages.
36791-the-mormon-puzzle-and-how-to-solve:
The Mormon Puzzle and How to Solve It, by Beers, is a polemical study. Funk and Wagnalls issued it in 1887, entered for rights in 1886. Beers served as Presbyterian pastor at Elkton, Maryland, when he wrote it. Next to the labor problem, he calls Mormonism America most pressing question then.

Two years of study, Mormon and non Mormon sources alike, back his case. Dickinson, Waite, Coyner, and the Schaff Herzog encyclopedia are named as aids. Short Utah visits warp most writers, he warns, into one sided views of it. His preface promises a fair, impartial probe of every phase of the problem. A plan to solve the puzzle is the book promised payoff.
36996-mystic-immanence-the-indwelling-sp:
Mystic Immanence, The Indwelling Spirit, is a devotional book by Basil Wilberforce, issued in 1914. Elliot Stock of Paternoster Row published the archdeacon small works in London. A works list prices his Secret of the Quiet Mind and Spiritual Consciousness volumes. Sermons preached in Westminster Abbey fill two of his listed series at five shillings.

Wilberforce, archdeacon of Westminster, taught that God dwells within the soul directly. Immanence, not distance, is the key word of his liberal Anglican mysticism in these pages. The book sold at eighteen pence, or in white parchment for half a crown. Edwardian devotion gains a mild, hopeful voice in this slight volume.
37592-neuralgia-and-the-diseases-that-re:
Neuralgia and the Diseases That Resemble It is a medical treatise by Francis Anstie. Bermingham of New York brought this edition out in the year 1882. Anstie was a fellow of the Royal College of Physicians in London. He served Westminster Hospital as senior assistant physician in his post. His preface claims a great need for an English treatise on neuralgia.

The work puts forward a substantially new view of the subject, he says. A brief sketch of it ran in Reynolds's System of Medicine before.
