Anstie vindicates neuralgia as a distinct and independent disease in itself. It is no mere offshoot of the gouty or rheumatic diatheses. Still less is it a chance symptom of a score of diseases. The second part arrays the spurious neuralgias as a gallery apart. Sorting true from false cases proved harder than most would guess.
37673-ned-wilding-s-disappearance-or-the:
Ned Wilding's Disappearance, or The Darewell Chums in the City, is a boys' tale by Allen Chapman. Chapman was the author of Bart Stirling's Road to Success and Bound to Succeed. The book carries a copyright date of 1908. Its contents list a run of out-door chapters first: The New Gun, Preparing for a Hunt, and Off in the Woods.

The First Turkey and The Blizzard stand next in the list, then A Lonely Cabin and Home for Thanksgiving. Getting Square with Sandy and Santa Claus in School stand later, and the list breaks off at Wreck of the T— in the part shown. The tale joins a hunt and a storm to the loss of its title figure and the chums' life in the city, as its twin titles state. It is a story of schoolboy friends and their trials.
37864-know-the-truth-a-critique-on-the-h:
Know the Truth is a critique by Jesse Jones of the Hamiltonian theory of limitation, with strictures on the theories of Henry Mansel and Herbert Spencer, published at New York in 1865. Jones dedicates the treatise to his fellow-students and friends of Andover Theological Seminary who had read Mansel and rejected his teachings.

The preface says the book was written simply in the interest of truth, against doctrines of the Hamiltonian school believed to be dangerous errors. In the final analysis, Jones argues, only two systems of philosophical theology are possible. One is pantheism, or atheism, the same principle viewed from different standpoints. The other is a pure theism. The argument that follows tests the schools by that division.
40208-life-of-thomas-paine-written-purpo:
A Life of Thomas Paine, written purposely to bind with his writings, is a memoir by Richard Carlile, in a second edition of 1821. Carlile states his aim at the start with care. Such a memoir is not a thing much wanted in itself, he grants. But custom makes it fitting for a set of an author's works to carry a brief account of his life.

That account should serve as a key to the author's mind, principles, and works, he says. It is the best general preface a reader could have. The compiler must not seek the praise of friends or the slander of enemies. Once an author has passed the bar of nature, judgment should rest on the writings he left behind. If those writings make him immortal, the life matters only through them.
41046-international-law-a-treatise-volum:
International Law is a treatise by Oppenheim, Whewell Professor of International Law at Cambridge. Longmans printed the second edition of Volume One, Peace, at London in 1912. Oppenheim dedicates the work to Edward Arthur Whittuck, whose sympathy accompanied it from inception to close. The first edition had appeared in 1905.

The preface explains the new edition's growth. Events since 1905, and the results of further research, forced a thorough revision. Some parts were rewritten outright. A number of new topics had to be discussed, and the additions lengthened the work considerably. New matter stands under separate headings and sections, so the reader can tell it from the old. Oppenheim's treatise became the standard English statement of the law of nations, and this Peace volume is its foundation stone.
41047-international-law-a-treatise-volum:
International Law: A Treatise, in its second volume, covers war and neutrality. L Oppenheim, Whewell Professor of International Law at Cambridge, wrote the work. Longmans, Green and Company published the second edition in London in 1912. The first volume treats peace, in the same systematic form.

The preface explains the scale of the revision. Events since 1906, when the volume first appeared, forced thorough changes. Many portions were rewritten and new topics added. Oppenheim writes as the leading positivist of his field. Rules are drawn from treaties and state practice, not from speculation. His treatise became the standard English authority on the law of nations. This volume's rules on war and neutral rights were tested within two years by the Great War itself.
4229-the-south-pole-an-account-of-the-no:
Roald Amundsen's account of the South Pole expedition follows the Norwegian party from Madeira to the Barrier and on to the Pole. Anchoring in Funchal Roads, the party waits for Amundsen's brother, who arrives by boat under their stern after they feared they had come first.

All is well aboard, the brother reports, and the voyage south resumes toward ice and winter quarters. Amundsen writes with a leader's plain care for ships, dogs, depots, and men. Readers who love polar adventure will find the first conquest of the Pole told by the man who won it.
42449-my-wonderful-visit:
My Wonderful Visit is Charlie Chaplin's account of his holiday trip to Europe. Hurst and Blackett published the book at London, with pictures. Chaplin had spent seven years under California's studio lights. A steak and kidney pie, the flu, and a cable start the tale, he jokes.

Chaplin opens by owning to homesickness and a wish for applause. He sails for England and walks the haunts of his poor childhood. A memorable night in London and meetings with famed men fill the middle. He sits with Thomas Burke and with Wells, the novelist. France and Germany follow, then a flight from Paris back to London. Farewells close the book at the ship. The visit was the silent star's first return home in triumph.
4267-abbeychurch-or-self-control-and-sel:
Charlotte M. Yonge first wrote this tale early in her career and later reissued it, with its faults intact, after readers kept asking for it. Set around a village church and its young people, the story contrasts self-control with self-conceit: the danger of doing one's duty in ninety-nine points and failing on the hundredth.

In her preface Yonge admits the book's exuberant historical allusions and its portrait of a passing phase, the so-called march of intellect among a set of girls. The novel's interest lies in its moral comedy, as clergymen, schoolgirls, and families argue over education, manners, and vulgarity, and learn how hard steady self-denial can be.
43132-the-little-old-portrait:
Mrs Molesworth wrote The Little Old Portrait, later called Edmee, a tale of the French Revolution, published in London by the Society for Promoting Christian Knowledge. An introduction opens in France, where the writer now writes. Nearly a hundred years ago this beautiful country was in a most sad and troubled state, she says. Lives passed in quiet times can scarcely picture it, she adds.

For hundreds of years the causes of the outbreak had been slowly growing, she holds. At last the storm broke all bounds, and the country was given to the rage of the mob, she says. Yet it would be unjust to blame the leaders and followers alone, she argues. In national as in family quarrels, faults on both sides is almost always true, she notes. Girls get a gentle tale set in the Terror.
43470-the-sinn-fein-rebellion-as-i-saw-i:
The Sinn Fein Rebellion As I Saw It is a set of true letters by Norway, the wife of the head clerk of the post in Ireland. It came out at London in the year of the rise. Prints fill it, and a copy of a stamp of the new free state stands on its cover.

A photo at its front shows the burnt shell of the great post house of Dublin, with its flag staff felled that bore the flag of the free state. She claims no craft of the pen for her words, the book owns. They were writ in a time of most strain, for kin eyes first, she says. They are a true hour by hour tale of the rise as she saw it, from the heart of the post rule of the land.
43626-curious-epitaphs-collected-from-th:
Curious Epitaphs is a gathering of odd gravestone verses copied from the burial grounds of Great Britain and Ireland. The collector is William Andrews, a fellow of the Royal Historical Society and secretary of the Hull Literary Club. The book was published at London by Hamilton, Adams, and Company, and carries life, family, and history notes with the stones.

In his preface Andrews says he collected epitaphs for many years and offers the fruit of his gleanings here. He stresses that the book was not compiled from earlier books. The verses were copied from the gravestones themselves. Some chapters first appeared under his name in Chambers's Journal and other papers. A list of epitaph books is included for readers who wish to go further.
4382-the-pit:
Frank Norris wrote this Chicago novel as the second part of his unfinished Trilogy of the Epic of the Wheat, after The Octopus. Set in 1903, it follows Curtis Jadwin, capitalist and speculator, Sheldon Corthell the artist, Landry Court the broker's clerk, and Samuel Gretry the broker. With them are Charles Cressler, dealer in grain, and Laura and Page Dearborn.

The pit of the title is the Chicago wheat pit, where fortunes are made and broken on the price of grain. Norris shows speculation as a force larger than any man, sweeping up lovers, artists, and dealers alike. The novel is a naturalist epic of business, vivid in its trading scenes and tragic in its outcome.
44431-four-hundred-humorous-illustration:
Four Hundred Humorous Illustrations, volume one, gathers comic drawings by George Cruikshank, with his portrait and a life sketch. The second edition came from Simpkin, Marshall, Hamilton, Kent and Company of London. The sketch opens the book and sets the plates in the frame of the artist's career.

Cruikshank was born in London on September 27, 1792. His father Isaac was an artist skilled in water colour and etching. His elder brother Isaac Robert also became an artist of note. The sketch holds that George struck out a new line from the first, with a vein of his own that experts could pick out. The plates show the comic force that made him famous.
44432-four-hundred-humorous-illustration:
Four Hundred Humorous Illustrations, by George Cruikshank, pairs his pictures with a portrait and a life. Simpkin and partners issued this second edition at London. A biographical sketch opens the volume. Cruikshank was born in London on September 27, 1792. His father Isaac was an artist skilled in water-colour and etching. His mother came from Perth, a Miss Macnaughten. She kept house with strong will and thrift, and raised the children in piety. The family lived in Duke Street, Bloomsbury, then Dorset Street by Fleet Street.

The mother coloured the father's plates by hand, with help from her sons. George and his elder brother Isaac Robert had little schooling. The father died in 1811 with a steady trade in stage designs and prints. The sketch frames the comic art that fills the book.
46032-vitus-bering-the-discoverer-of-ber:
Peter Lauridsen wrote Vitus Bering, the Discoverer of Bering Strait. Julius E Olson translated it from the Danish. S C Griggs and Company issued it at Chicago in 1889. Lauridsen sat on Denmark's geographical council. He edited Jens Munk's northern voyage as well. Frederick Schwatka wrote the American intro.

Russian Explorations, 1725-1743 heads the contents part. Bering's First Expedition fills Part One there. Russia and England in Arctic work open it. Bering's rank as explorer gets weighed first. His birth and the Danes under Peter follow. Peter the Great founded Russia's navy then. Plans for the first expedition fill chapter three. Peter wished to know his empire's extent, it says. The Northeast Passage was his great question there. A Danish life of the great north explorer brought Russian charts and Siberian roads to English readers.
47519-president-heber-c-kimball-s-journa:
Heber Kimball's Journal is the seventh book of the Faith-Promoting Series. The Juvenile Instructor office printed it at Salt Lake City in 1882. The series aimed to instruct and encourage young Latter-day Saints. The journal covers Kimball's mission to England. Chapter one tells of his call, his appointment to preside, and the journey. Chapter two admits his timidity at the size of the task.

Prompted by the spirit, he went to Preston to preach. A minister invited him into a chapel, then closed its doors when his craft seemed endangered. Another minister forbade him to baptize church members. A desperate struggle with evil spirits is also recorded. Baptisms began, and the elders separated to widen the work. Later chapters tell of the first conference in England. The Word of Wisdom was first taught there, the contents note.
47532-the-catacombs-of-rome-and-their-te:
The Catacombs of Rome, by Withrow, studies the burial caves of early Christians. Hodder and Stoughton issued it at London in 1888 with many plates. Its full title adds their testimony relative to primitive Christianity as scope. Withrow wrote for general readers shut out from costly foreign folios on it.

New digs had refuted old theories, so a fresh English account was due. Pagan grave inscriptions and church fathers light up early Christian life here. Hundreds of early Christian inscriptions appear in translation, many new to English. Doctor McCaul revised most of those renderings with a scholar care throughout. A Protestant view guides the reading of the latest results.
47765-a-profitable-instruction-of-the-pe:
A Profitable Instruction of the Perfect Ordering of Bees, by Thomas Hyll of London, is an early English beekeeping manual. Henrie Bynneman printed it at London in 1579, in the old spelling of its day. Hyll's full title promises the marvellous nature, property and government of bees, and the necessary uses of their honey and wax, inward and outward.

Hyll gathered his matter, he says, out of the best writers. His list of authors runs from Pliny and Aristotle to Cato, Columella, Varro and Palladius. A second treatise is annexed, on husbandly conjectures of dearth and plenty for ever. The transcriber warns that its final four chapters are absent, and that no known copy of the edition is complete. The book is among the first bee manuals printed in English.
47992-in-the-misty-seas-a-story-of-the-s:
In the Misty Seas, a story of the sealers of Behring Strait, is a sea novel by Harold Bindloss, printed at London. The frontispiece carries a warning speech: tell your skipper that if ever his schooner is found inside our limits again, the speaker will have much pleasure in sinking her. Six illustrations go with the tale.

The first chapter, Jimmy's Duck, opens at Sandycombe School, where Bluey the Nova Scotian sits up on his pillow and talks of the sea. Out of dock, down Channel, and a lesson in seamanship follow. The Champlain, sealer, comes into the tale, with a trial of speed and the picking up of the boats. Stickine makes a deal, the pledge is redeemed, and treachery leads to the sealers' reckoning. The last chapter is called The Result of the Choice.
49145-remarks-upon-the-first-report-of-t:
Remarks upon the First Report of the Royal Commission on Ritual is a church lecture. Mayow, incumbent of St Mary's at West Brompton, gave the lecture himself. He spoke at Brighton on November 27, 1867, to the English Church Union. Barchard sat in the chair for that annual meeting of the branch. The Church Press Company published the lecture in London in 1868.

Mayow ties ritual questions to the integrity of the Book of Common Prayer. The Brighton branch asked leave to print his words for wider use. He also gave the same lecture at Bradford and at Leeds. Church parties then fought hard over rite, vestment, and prayer book text. Union men heard in Mayow a defence of their ritual cause in full.
50325-the-castle-of-ehrenstein-its-lords:
The Castle of Ehrenstein, its lords spiritual and temporal, its inhabitants earthly and unearthly, a novel by G P R James, was issued at Leipzig by Bernhard Tauchnitz in 1847. It is volume one hundred fifteen of the Collection of British Authors, in a copyright edition for the continent. James was among the most prolific novelists of his day. A storm over a German castle opens the tale.

Lightning crosses the rain and shows the black forest and broken rocks like spectres of a world gone by. Toward one in the morning a young man of about twenty one steals through the great halls with a small brazen lamp. He is well born but poor for his class, and wears a heavy sword though the times are peaceful. His grave errand, and the castle's lords and ghosts, carry the romance.
50895-the-rat-pit:
The Rat-Pit is a novel of Irish poverty by Patrick MacGill. Doran published the book at New York in 1915. The contents run to thirty five chapters. The tale follows Norah and her people from a Donegal cabin to work across the water.

The first chapter opens an hour before dawn in midwinter. A mother checks her girl's brogues and her brown penny for tea and bread. The cabin has no light and no warmth, and sleet beats through the broken window. The tide is turning, and Norah must be off to the town. Later chapters treat school life, a wake, and the train to Derry. Drudgery, little loves, and a rag store fill the middle. MacGill wrote from his own youth as a hired farm boy.
51039-the-laws-and-principles-of-whist-s:
The Laws and Principles of Whist, by the writer who signs as Cavendish, reached an eighteenth edition in 1889. Thomas De La Rue of London printed that edition, and all rights were reserved. The book is given to James Clay, chairman of the Whist Laws Committee of the Arlington Club in 1864.

The frontispiece, Ruff and Honours, is borrowed from the Compleat Gamester of 1680. Its verse shows ladies at the card table shooting Cupid's darts from their eyes. Partners, the joke runs, lose their game and their hearts at once. The title page states the book's method. The laws and principles of the game are stated and explained. Their practice is then shown on an original system, by means of hands played through. A learner thus gets rule and example on the same plan, rather than bare rules alone.
51197-what-to-eat-how-to-serve-it:
What to Eat, How to Serve It is a household guide by Christine Terhune Herrick, author of Housekeeping Made Easy. Harper and Brothers published it at New York in 1891. The first chapter treats the dining room, the room where the family gathers three times a day. Herrick bids it be pleasant, since there is no escaping it as there is from other rooms.

The contents run through the whole day and year. Breakfast chapters cover the family table, the invalid's breakfast, and breakfasts for each season. Luncheon, the lunch basket, and dinners at night, at noon, and on Sunday follow, with small and large parties. A chapter asks what shall we eat, and others treat the children's table, teas, china and glass, and linen and silver.
51534-self-portrait:
Self Portrait is a science fiction story by Bernard Wolfe. The Project Gutenberg text was taken from Galaxy Science Fiction for November 1951, with pictures by Martin Schneider. Its headnote speaks of a cyberneticist who thought nothing too good for his fellow scientists. Much too good for them, it adds.

The tale is told as a diary. On October 5, 1959, the writer, Parks, arrives at Princeton. His new post is at a place called IFACS, which he calls quite a place. The staff look like college boys in dungarees and sweatshirts. They lounge on the grass and chalk equations in the conference rooms. Many of them, he guesses, work in the secret end of the place, the MS end. His boss tells him he has come to the most important address in America, the Pentagon not excepted.
51809-survival-kit:
Survival Kit is a science fiction story by Frederik Pohl. It was printed in Galaxy Science Fiction in May 1957. The pictures are by Gaughan. The story opens on the Jersey shore in a December gale.

Mooney looks out of his window and the sky goes white in a sudden, bright, cold flare. He decides it is none of his business. Mooney is living alone in a summer house left by his Uncle Lester. He keeps all four burners and the oven going, wears a scarf and a heavy jacket indoors, and lives on tea, cookies and canned goods. He has been on that diet for three weeks, with solitaire and television to pass the nights. Pohl builds the tale from that cold, spare setting, as the flare in the sky turns into something Mooney cannot leave alone.
52309-twenty-two-goblins-translated-from:
Twenty-Two Goblins holds tales turned from the Sanskrit by Arthur W Ryder. The book came out in 1917, with twenty plates in colour by Perham W Nahl. A goblin poses a hard question at the end of each tale.

One tale asks whose fault a death was after a prince's flight with his bride. In a second, three lovers each help bring a dead girl back to life. The riddle asks which of them should wed her. A parrot and a thrush debate which sex is worse, men or women. Each short tale ends with a knot the hearer must untie. Ryder's plain English keeps the old tales brisk and clear.
5313-the-herd-boy-and-his-hermit:
Charlotte M. Yonge's Herd Boy and His Hermit opens with Southey's verses on Henry of Windsor. The holy king upon whose head ancestral crimes were visited, meek and patient, blessing while he kissed the rod. Its contents move from the moss and a snowstorm, over the moor, to a sporting prioress, mother and son, a cautious stepfather, and Derwent banks.

Later chapters bring the hermit himself, Henry of Windsor, a scholar of the mountains, the red rose, and fellow travellers on a journey. Yonge writes a historical tale of medieval England, where a herd boy's life crosses a saintly king's, in her usual moral and domestic manner.
54176-the-cremation-of-the-dead-consider:
Hugo Erichsen, a doctor, argues for the burning of the dead in place of burial. His book came out at Detroit in 1887. Sir Spencer Wells, a famed surgeon, wrote a note at the front.

Erichsen treats his theme from six points of view in turn. He weighs looks, health, faith, the past and the law. Cost to the living gets a full share as well. His motto in Latin calls for burial to be ended. A quote from Washington Irving asks why the tomb should be ringed with dread. The book is a bold plea for reform. Plates of a modern urn show the new rite in practice.
55048-the-retreat-from-mons-by-one-who-s:
The Retreat from Mons, by one who shared in it, is a war memoir by Corbett-Smith, an artillery major, published by Cassell at London in 1916 with three plates and a map. It is dedicated to General Smith-Dorrien.

The preface explains that the author first meant to trace the war through Smith-Dorrien's command of the Second Army, from Mons to Ypres. One phase, the retreat itself, had gripped the public imagination beyond every other event of the past two years, and people knew almost nothing of it. Yet the story can never be told as it should, he warns: only those who lived its horror and splendour could tell it, and for them the facts are blurred by nightmare. He writes instead of the big human side, the trivial, homely incidents of the British soldier's daily life.
55128-extempore-speech-how-to-acquire-an:
William Pittenger wrote Extempore Speech, a manual issued in Philadelphia in 1883. Pittenger taught at the National School of Elocution and Oratory. The subtitle promises to show how to acquire and practice the art. His earlier book, Oratory, Sacred and Secular, held the same views in rougher form.

The preface denies that a book on eloquence must itself be eloquent. A man may describe an eagle's flight while standing on firm ground. Pittenger offers plain directions on practical details instead. He trusts them to serve the highest genius and the plain speaker alike. His method joins two habits. Thought must be prepared and arranged with care. Words, though, should be chosen on the spot as one speaks. Nine in ten fair speakers, he holds, will do best this way.
55174-oratory-sacred-and-secular-or-the-:
Oratory Sacred and Secular, or The Extemporaneous Speaker, by William Pittenger, author of Daring and Suffering, was published in New York in 1869. John Bingham wrote the opening essay, and an appendix gives a chairman's guide for running public meetings on the best parliamentary models. Sketches of the most famed speakers of all ages fill much of the book.

Pittenger says he began public speaking with no manual to warn him of pitfalls or guide self-training. Such help would have saved him hard lessons and sped his progress in the art of coining thought into words. He treats general preparation at full length, as the base on which all special work rests, drawing on Bautain, Stevens, and Holyoake.
55300-society-as-i-have-found-it:
Society as I Have Found It is the memoir of Ward McAllister, the arbiter of New York fashion, copyrighted in 1890. Cassell of New York published the book. A signed portrait of the author fronts the volume. Two mottoes on memoirs and individuality head the text.

McAllister declares his book miscellaneous, with a noble disdain of regularity. He asks how a man makes his memoirs interesting at the start. Individuality is not quite enough, he answers, it must be made felt in writing. McAllister coined the phrase the Four Hundred for New York’s chosen set. His pages name the balls, dinners, and rules of that gilded world. Hostesses read him as gospel, and enemies as evidence. The memoir is the source book of Gilded Age society.
55496-a-household-book-of-english-poetry:
A Household Book of English Poetry was chosen and set in order by Richard Chenevix Trench, printed in London in 1868. Trench was Archbishop of Dublin. He added notes to the poems. In his preface he asks if Palgrave's Golden Treasury left room for a new book. He decides it did, since his plan differs. Of more than three hundred pieces here, fewer than seventy appear in Palgrave's set.

Trench takes in all kinds of poetry, not just songs and lyrics. He also admits living poets, where Palgrave did not. His aim is not to be full or complete. He gives a few samples even of the best poets. The book suits home reading and study of English verse across a wide span.
55534-the-aeroplane-express-or-the-boy-a:
The Aeroplane Express is a boys' aviation novel by Ashton Lamar. It is the third book of the Aeroplane Boys series. Reilly and Britton of Chicago issued the series. The first volume puts Morey Marshall in the Signal Corps. The second tells how Bud Wilson made good. This one is subtitled The Boy Aeronaut's Grit. A colour frontispiece shows two pistol shots in the desert.

The contents move from a bargain to a desert flight. An ancestor is looked up in the third chapter. The trail is found at the San Juan canyon. A white god of the sink hole adds a mystery. An aeroplane is assembled in the desert itself. Such series sold flying as the newest boy heroism. Correct detail was promised on the wrapper. The books cost sixty cents in cloth.
56285-the-oyster-where-how-and-when-to-f:
An unnamed author wrote a full guide to the oyster, its beds, and its table use. Trubner and Company issued the book in London in the Roman year MDCCCLXI. A plate of ancient Britons camped near Colchester fronts the work. Billingsgate trade and London demand open the survey.

Chapters trace Greek and Roman feasts, Sergius Orata's beds, and British Rutupian fame. Whitstable, Colchester, Dublin, and Poole beds get close local study. Roasted, fried, stewed, and scalloped forms close the book with soups and sauces. Cooks and traders of the time gain lore, history, and recipes in one small book.
56468-nunnery-life-in-the-church-of-engl:
Sister Mary Agnes wrote Nunnery Life in the Church of England, or Seventeen Years with Father Ignatius, edited with a preface by Rev W Lancelot Holland. Hodder and Stoughton in London issued the book in MDCCCXCI, in its fifth thousand. A photogravure portrait of the sister heads the volume. Seventeen chapters and three appendices fill the tale. Her reasons for becoming a sister stand first.

Convent life entered upon, then the vows of poverty, chastity, and obedience follow. Life at Feltham Convent, at Slapton in Devonshire, and at Llanthony fill the middle. Daily routine at Llanthony, ill treatment of children, and Llanthony rules with penances expose the house. Her departure, a return, apparitions and miracles, and liberty close the memoir. Church readers get an ex nun account of Father Ignatius order.
56598-harry-coverdale-s-courtship-and-al:
Frank Smedley wrote a novel of country life and courtship that Routledge of London published in 1854. Chapter two shows Harry Coverdale at work among his tenants. He and his friend Hazlehurst have walked six hours by two in the day and shot seven couple of rabbits between them. A rich lunch waits at the gamekeeper's cottage.

Hazlehurst, softened by London life, is worn out by the tramp through grass and fern. Coverdale, kindly, sends for a pony to carry him home. He asks after a tenant named Styles on the way. The keeper calls Styles a tall, rough customer, hard to tackle, with a lurcher dog at his heel. The scene sets Harry in his place, a young squire at ease with gun, tenants, and land, before the courtship of the title begins.
56821-four-phases-of-morals-socrates-ari:
John Stuart Blackie, professor of Greek in the University of Edinburgh, wrote Four Phases of Morals, here in a second edition issued at Edinburgh in 1874. The four phases are Socrates, Aristotle, Christianity, and the utility school. Blackie first gave the matter as lectures before the Royal Institution in London in the season of 1869, where the course was held to four talks.

In his letter at the front he owns that four phases give a fragment of the whole field of ethics. He chose the historical path over bare argument, taking each phase in its concrete form. The talks aim at the deep questions of right and conduct through the men and creeds that shaped them. Blackie dedicated the book to Henry Holland of the Royal Institution.
56957-a-history-of-the-irish-poor-law-in:
Sir George Nicholls wrote this history of the Irish poor law and the state of the Irish people. Nicholls knew the theme from the inside: he had shaped poor relief in England and was sent to frame it for Ireland. His name stands large on the title page.

Ireland's poor law was young and fiercely fought when he wrote. The workhouse test, the rates, and the great famine's shadow all hang over such a history. Nicholls tells how relief grew from parish charity to a set law with unions and boards. He ties the law's tale to the people's real state: their cabins, food, and work. Part record, part plea, it is a first source for a grim theme.
5771-the-art-of-the-exposition-personal-:
Eugen Neuhaus records personal impressions of the Panama-Pacific International Exposition in The Art of the Exposition. Neuhaus, of the University of California and a member of the San Francisco jury, treats architecture, sculpture, mural decoration, color scheme, and other aesthetic aspects of the fair. His account is avowedly personal, offering judgment rather than a mere catalogue.

Readers walk the fair through an expert eye, learning why courts, palaces, and color choices worked together. The book pairs well with guides to the exposition's sculpture, since Neuhaus judges the whole visual effect. Lovers of World's Fair history, California art, and early twentieth-century design will find a thoughtful, firsthand record of a fleeting city built to delight.
5791-mrs-peter-rabbit:
Burgess follows Peter Rabbit's search for a mate in Mrs Peter Rabbit, opening with Peter losing his appetite. Chapters send Peter planning a journey, watch Hooty the Owl change hunting grounds, and follow a shadow with sharp claws into the old pasture. Peter stays lonesome, finds tracks, meets an unpleasant surprise, and almost decides to return home before his quest resolves.

Young readers find woodland neighbors, seasonal dangers, and gentle lessons about patience and courage. Burgess writes in short chapters suited to bedtime, with animal characters who think and feel in human ways. The book suits early readers and read-aloud families, and it continues the Green Meadow world that made Burgess a favorite children's author.
58461-reading-how-to-teach-it:
Reading: How to Teach It is a guide for teachers by Sarah Louise Arnold. Arnold was supervisor of schools in Boston when she wrote it. Silver, Burdett and Company brought it out in 1899. She had written Stepping Stones to Literature and Waymarks for Teachers before. The book asks teachers to dignify a task they do each day.

Her greeting tells the teacher to keep the end goal in sight. Small first steps in reading must point toward a goal worth striving for. The child does not see that end from the start, she notes. Still, the teacher must see it and guide each plain lesson by it. These pages try to state the true import of teaching reading. They aim to help teachers prize their work and do it well.
59255-easy-does-it:
E G Von Wald wrote a science fiction tale that ran in Worlds of If in May 1955. Hal Webber sits in a soft Formair executive's chair that supports him perfectly in every position. Suspend field furniture, the tale notes, is the best made. Yet Hal feels a puzzled frown and a lurking tension he cannot explain.

His father enters to announce a new coloration process. It will, he says, quintuple the family fortune within a year. They may be the richest people in the world. Hal answers mildly, with strange emphasis. The head note sets up a later stranding in the wilderness with a beautiful girl, where Hal's conditioning is off.
59498-what-shall-it-profit:
Poul Anderson wrote a tale of men made idle by machines. What Shall It Profit ran in Worlds of If Science Fiction in June 1956. A quote at the front warns to count the cost before building a tower. Barwell drinks in a booth as dice rattle and music whines nearby.

Barwell faces the dole, here called citizen's credit, from tomorrow on. No work he can do beats a machine, he says with bitter cheer. Radek calls himself adaptable and needles his friend's despair. Readers gain a sharp, sad look at pride and worth in a world of plenty.
59650-the-new-teaching-of-history-with-a:
H G Wells wrote The New Teaching of History, a plea for one world tale. Cassell and Company issued the book in London in nineteen hundred twenty one. A reply to attacks on his Outline of History stands with the plea. Two hundred thousand buyers had taken the Outline by then.

Three years Wells spent in putting his own past views in order. Checked by many hands, the Outline gave all time as one tale. Its frame lets each reader hang his own lore in its place, he holds. Its wide vogue sprang from a wide thirst, not his lone gift, he owns. Any bold hand might have met that long felt want as well, he says. Some attacks yet teach much on how schools should teach the past. Notes on those points fill this short, keen companion book.
6001-polly-of-pebbly-pit:
Lillian Elizabeth Roy sends Polly Brewster to a ranch-house farm in Pebbly Pit, where a musical call from the kitchen doorway finds her kneeling beside her pet in the barn. Her father tells her to run and see what Maw wants, and the tale opens on farm chores and family talk.

Chapters follow with a momentous letter, preparing for the unknown, the servant problem solved, city girls acclimated, a dance at Bear Forks, and a blizzard on Grizzly Slide. A night in a cave and old Montresor's legacy deepen the adventure. Roy mixes ranch work, mishaps, and plucky girlhood.
60489-a-short-treatise-on-the-section-of:
A Short Treatise on the Section of the Prostate Gland in Lithotomy is a medical work by Charles Aston Key. Key was surgeon to Guy's Hospital and to the Magdalen in London. The book was printed at London by Longman and others. Its title page promises an account of a safe and easy method of carrying out the operation. The method rests on the principles of Cheselden, the great surgeon of the century before.

The work is illustrated by engravings. Lithotomy was the cutting for the stone, one of the few great operations of the time. The cut through the prostate gland was its most delicate step, and the point on which methods differed. Key writes as a hospital surgeon for other surgeons.
60935-don-t-think-about-it:
Do Not Think About It, a science fiction tale by William Stuart, ran in Worlds of If in 1960. A head note teases that the secret is not much of one, but the only one. The trick goes untold in that blurb at the top of the tale. Tommy, its child hero, was not really a timid child at all.

Sometimes he did not understand things and was puzzled, the tale begins of him. More often grown ups could not understand things clear to him, it goes on. Then mother and father turned his bafflement into silly adult terms of fear. The hole in the closet, when Tommy was just over three, opens his case. Mr Bear was afraid, and the thing puzzled Tommy enough to ask about it. A child with a strange gift hides in plain sight in this tale.
61053-tolliver-s-orbit:
Fyfe wrote a science fiction tale that ran in Worlds of If in September 1961. Johnny Tolliver scowls across a desk at his boss on Ganymede. He did not ask Jeffers to cut out his own graft, he says. He knows Jeffers runs something sneaky through the colony, but it is not for him.

Jeffers, the moon faced manager of the Ganymede branch of Koslow Spaceways, glowers back. A little percentage on cargoes never shows by the time figures reach Earth, he growls. The big jets at home count it in estimates anyway. Tolliver is pulled off the Callisto run on the spot. The slow orbit of the title becomes his dull new post, and his honesty its risk.
61168-the-man-in-the-brown-suit:
The Man in the Brown Suit, by Agatha Christie, was published in New York in nineteen twenty-four by Dodd, Mead and Company. Christie's earlier books, The Mysterious Affair at Styles, The Secret Adversary, and The Murder on the Links, are listed on the title leaf. She dedicates the novel to E A B, in memory of a journey and some lion stories.

The prologue opens on Nadina, a Russian dancer who had taken Paris by storm. Her manager kisses her on both cheeks as the curtain falls on scarlet and magenta. The dedication asks for the mystery of the mill house, which this story answers in its own way. Anne Beddingfeld, Christie's narrator, soon takes the tale to South Africa. The book is her fourth novel and her most romantic, a thriller of diamonds and disguises.
61204-the-recruit:
The Recruit is a tale by Bryce Walton. It was put out in Worlds of If Science Fiction in July 1962. The head note sets its theme in brief: it was dirty work, but it would make him a man. And kids had a right to grow up, some of them, the note adds, with a grim twist.

The tale opens with Wayne, unseen, sneering down from the head of the stairs. The old man below has a thick neck, a thick cigar, an evening drink, and a bald head with no brain in it, in the boy's view. His slim mother wears a polite smile and a fluttering voice. They are squareheads one and all, to Wayne, marking time in a gray dream. Man, was he glad to break out, the boy thinks, as the tale sets its young recruit in flight from home.
6138-life-and-habit:
Samuel Butler's Life and Habit returns in a 1910 edition with addenda and a preface by R. A. Streatfeild, thirty-three years after its first publication in 1878. Streatfeild notes years fruitful in change, when many mighty were put down and many humble exalted, and Butler himself exalted with unforeseen rapidity.

Butler, he says, can scarcely be called humble, having few misgivings about his ultimate triumph, yet his rise surprised even him. The book, inscribed to Charles Paine Pauli for criticism of proofs and old friendship, argues about habit, memory, and inheritance. It remains a bold, idiosyncratic work of Victorian thought.
61964-an-essay-on-the-state-of-england-i:
Essay on the State of England is a trade pamphlet by John Cary, printed at Bristol in 1695. Cary was a merchant of Bristol writing on trade, the poor, and taxes. The war against France then running gives the pamphlet its pressing occasion. A dedication to the king pleads no desire to appear in print as its motive.

True affection to his native country moved him, and the cause the king was engaged in. On that war hang religion, liberty, and property for all Protestant Europe, he argues. Workhouses for the poor and care of trade made Cary name in policy. Economic historians count the essay among the founding texts of English mercantilism.
62299-a-discourse-on-trade-and-other-mat:
Discourse on Trade is a vast economic pamphlet on English trade and its improvement. Its contents promise trade in general and the trade of England first in order. Husbandry, feeding, tillage, corn, fruit, fish, minerals, and trees follow in the bill. Manufactures from wool to silk, glass, paper mills, and powder mills fill the middle.

A universal national bank is demonstrated as a great advantage in the discourse. Employing the poor to improve manufactures and courts of merchants get their schemes. Trade to the Indies, Africa, the plantations, and all Europe is weighed for profit. Mercantilist England speaks at full length in this crowded table of contents.
62489-the-corner-house-girls-solve-a-mys:
Grace Brooks Hill wrote The Corner House Girls Solve a Mystery, published by Barse and Hopkins in New York in 1923. Thelma Gooch drew the pictures. The subtitle promises the whole method: what it was, where it was, and who found it. Hill's series followed the Kenway sisters of the corner house, and this volume gives the younger girls, Tess and Dot, a mystery of their own.

The contents promise witches and warlocks, a midnight tryst, and a strange summons. A frontispiece shows a timid Chinese man stepping out of moonlight shadows. Chapters end with Hop Wong caught, another alarm, and the capture. The story opens in the kitchen, where Sammy Pinkney's shout nearly makes Tess drop the cake batter. From such homely ground the girls investigate noises, notes, and midnight visitors. Hill wrote the kind of series mystery that girls of the nineteen twenties passed from hand to hand.
62684-the-belt-of-seven-totems-a-story-o:
The Belt of Seven Totems, a story of Massasoit by Kirk Munroe, was published at Philadelphia in 1901. The metadata names another writer, but the title page and copyright name Munroe. Emlen McConnell drew the pictures. Munroe tells readers the tale is not a history. He aims to reconcile clashing facts and explain a puzzling case. Why did Massasoit let the Pilgrims stay, after white men had wronged his people so often?

A plate shows a captive seized and dragged inboard by strong hands. The book forms part of a line of tales boys liked, printed here in a ninth impression. Munroe had written Under the Great Bear and other sea and land stories. His tale gives young readers a dramatic view of first contact in New England.
63621-my-little-bit:
My Little Bit, by Marie Corelli, author of Barabbas and Romance of Two Worlds, was copyrighted in 1919 and published in New York by Doran. Corelli dedicates the book to a friend and his fellow members of the Carlton Club. Some sixty short pieces, most from the war years, run from England, 1918 and Savage Glory through For Belgium, The Kaiser's Harvest of Death, and Starving Belgium.

Later pieces take up sea power from 1805 to 1918, the appeal for the French Red Cross, the war loan, food production, hoarding, and the women's vote. Shakespeare's war birthday in 1917 gets a piece of its own. The opening poem lifts its eyes to England as queen warrior of the world. Corelli's little bit was morale in print: verse and prose meant to stiffen a tired nation's heart.
63837-peril-orbit:
Peril Orbit is a science fiction story by C J Wedlake, taken from Planet Stories for the summer of 1949. Its pilot, Jim MacDonald, flies a tiny one-man ship alone. The hook asks why his training will not let him give up, caught in the sun.

MacDonald had used the sun's pull to sling his ship from Earth toward Venus when a space warp funneled out and caught him. He escaped the warp by flawless reckoning, but the price was everything: his fuel spent just as his jet tubes melted. Now the ship swings fuelless in a tight orbit with a slight inward drift. Inside, the heat climbs past one hundred and forty-five degrees and the cooling system has long given up. Radio from beside the sun is jabber into static. He keeps his log anyway, and waits.
64447-buffalo-bill-s-pursuit:
Buffalo Bill's Pursuit, or The Heavy Hand of Justice, is a Western dime novel by Colonel Prentiss Ingraham. Street and Smith printed it at New York with copyright in 1907. Ingraham wrote the celebrated Buffalo Bill stories of the Border Stories line. An appreciation of William Cody opens the volume.

Thirty-one chapters run from The Voice from the Tree to the defeat of the Blackfeet. Pizen Jane of Cinnabar, a desert hotspur, and an outlaw stronghold fill the middle. There are captures, escapes, and a living barricade. The scouts' pursuit closes the tale. Ingraham, who knew Cody himself, keeps the pace of the old weekly stories.
64490-stories-of-the-wars-of-the-jews-fr:
A L O E, a writer of tales for the young, compiled Stories of the Wars of the Jews, issued by Nelson and Sons at London in 1900 with forty-four pictures. The tale runs from the Babylonish captivity to the fall of Jerusalem under Titus. Her preface names her sources: the Holy Scriptures, the books of the Apocrypha, and Josephus and his Wars of the Jews. She also used the writings of Prideaux and a small history of the Hebrews printed in India.

She holds that no history is fuller of lessons than that of God's chosen nation. Its annals show courage, faith, and self-giving, and also falling away and crime. The front picture shows Mordecai mourning. The book retells the wars of the Jewish people for Christian readers, as a tale of God's mercy and justice toward his people.
65914-shaming-the-speed-limit:
Shaming the Speed Limit is a novel by Burt Standish. Its first chapter, headed a girl, a dog, and a man, opens under a spreading oak in a pasture. Miss Elizabeth Wiggin settled herself snugly in the shade, the first lines say. She looked forward to a pleasant, quiet hour with her book, a romance whose title is given in full.

As may be guessed from that title, Miss Wiggin was romantic, the narrator adds. She was just eighteen, and the daughter of a judge of the village in the valley below. On fine afternoons she wandered off with only an aged sheep dog, hunting a spot to read without being broken in on. For her grim old father held trashy love stories in horror. Her aunt, a grave spinster who kept his house, held all such fiction in still deeper scorn.
65987-strength-and-how-to-obtain-it:
Strength and How to Obtain It is the exercise manual of Eugen Sandow, the strongman who founded modern bodybuilding. Gale and Polden published this revised edition in London at two shillings and sixpence net. An anatomical chart illustrates the exercises for physical development, and full-page portraits show Sandow and some of his pupils.

Sandow's introduction states his gospel plainly. He takes it as a commonplace, he writes, that everyone, man, woman and child, wants to be strong. By strength he means health, vitality and a general sense of physical well-being, without which life is a gloomy business. Wealth, talent and the love of friends may console a man for lacking it, but they can never make up for it. Even readers whose condition rules out athletics, he promises, need not despair: they can reach a state fit to enjoy life.
66272-babies-are-such-fun-to-dress-sizes:
Babies Are Such Fun to Dress is Star Book number 220. The American Thread Company issued the pattern book. Its price was thirty five cents. Sizes run from six months to four years. Knit and crochet patterns fill the pages. Dawn yarns, in Orlon or baby wool, are named throughout. Say it with Daisies leads the sets. A puff stitch baby set, sized six to nine months, opens it. Seven one ounce skeins of white are called for. Crochet hooks in two sizes make the work. Gauges are given for each hook before a stitch is worked.

The sacque starts at the neck edge with a chain of eighty one. Sleeves, back, and fronts grow from increase points. The puff stitch pattern then carries the little coat to length. Photographs show babies wearing each set.
66707-meeting-at-the-summit:
Ivar Jorgensen wrote the tale Meeting At The Summit. Imagination magazine ran it in February 1956. A press secretary seeks the President late one night. Few men reach the President direct, the tale notes. This aide is a trusted friend as well. A buffer stands between the chief and the press in him.

The President bids him come right up by phone. A western tale book lies by the President's hand. He thumbs it, then sets it down again. Rest comes seldom to him these days. Golf fills most of his spare hours now. The world's mad dash to ruin fills the rest. A cold war beats a hot one, he muses. The cold war softens a bit, he judges. Top-level Cold War fiction, the tale trades rockets for talk at the very top of power.
67648-forty-years-of-it:
Forty Years of It is the autobiography of Brand Whitlock, published by D Appleton and Company of New York and London in 1914. Whitlock dedicated the book to the memory of his father, Elias D Whitlock, a minister who died on the twenty-third of December 1913. The narrative covers the author's first forty years, from small-town boyhood toward his public career.

It opens on a hot afternoon in the summer of his tenth year. His grandfather, having finished the nap he always took after the heavy noon dinner, lets the boy go up town with him. Whitlock recalls that such trips always ended in a present, more costly than the small rewards given at home. The memoir grew from magazine pieces and carries a reporter's eye for American town life.
67703-the-master-spirit:
Sir William Magnay wrote The Master Spirit, published by Little, Brown and Company at Boston in 1906. John Cameron drew the illustrations. Magnay was the author of The Red Chancellor and A Prince of Lovers. The frontispiece shows a man asking Alexia whether the time has come. The chapters open with a dweller in darkness and the history of a compact. A society sensation and the ducal point of view follow.

The man who guessed and the man behind lead to a fiery ordeal. The Vaux House case and Alexia's denial come next. Herriard and Alexia, a Mayfair counsellor, and a deepening tragedy fill the middle. The mask falls, and Herriard's confession comes late. A face in the box and a portent close the tale. The first chapter opens as a late sitting at Westminster empties into the night.
67717-bee-keeping-for-profit:
Bee-Keeping for Profit, by Morley, was published by Cassell at London in 1914. Eight plates illustrate the small handbook for smallholders and cottagers. General information and hints open the contents at page three. Hives and bee keepers requisites follow as the next two chapters of the guide.

Bees, their habits and products, then flowers and bees, fill the middle heads. Hints on working the bees run through two long chapters of practice. Feeding, securing the harvest of the hive, and diseases of bees follow in the list. Enemies of the bee and bee keeper close the contents before the index. Only in recent years, the introduction says, has bee keeping won a scientific basis. Old traditional methods once ruled the honey harvest without a known why or how.
67919-three-addresses-on-the-relations-s:
Three Addresses on the Relations Subsisting between the White and Colored People of the United States is a pamphlet of speeches by Frederick Douglass. Printers in Washington issued the work in 1886. The first address was given at a convention of colored men at Louisville in September 1883. Douglass spoke for delegates chosen from all parts of the country.

The opening address asks fair play for a people lately enslaved. It notes that the freed still suffer from the evils of their former state. Chief among those evils is the low and unjust view white citizens take of their worth. Douglass argues that relations between the races rest more on habits of thought than on courts or creeds. He congratulates the nation that slavery, a two century reproach, has been blotted out.
68406-essay-on-the-effects-of-iodine-on-:
Essay on the Effects of Iodine on the Human Constitution, by Gairdner, is a medical treatise on a new drug. Underwood printed it in London in 1824, at Fleet Street. Its full title adds practical notes on iodine's use against three diseases.

Those diseases are bronchocele, scrophula, and the tubercular ills of chest and belly. The introduction warns that the drug is new and little understood. Most doctors have heard of its power over bronchocele, Gairdner says. Some, rashly taking it for a weak drug, have dosed without study of its dangers. He has seen doctors ruined in name and patients ruined in health by it. One London doctor gave ten grains at a dose to a young woman. Vomiting saved her, the essay reports. Another case shows a surgeon bleeding a dying girl, then reaching for drug after drug.
69216-sheared-cream-o-wit-a-classified-c:
Sheared Cream o' Wit is an anthology of jokes, quips, and light verse, gathered by Mittler of Louisville, Kentucky. It was copyrighted in 1923. The compiler says he spent forty years picking the pieces, first for himself and a small circle of friends.

A letter at the front warns the reader in rhyme. Rich food gulped down brings indigestion, so take these treasures a little at a time. The foreword counts the book's uses. Under the evening lamp a family may laugh together. A tired business man may rest his mind in office or train. The sick in hospital may cheer their hours of waiting. After-dinner speakers may find stories to steal. The title tells the aim: the cream of wit, sheared from a wide field.
69959-your-vote-and-how-to-use-it:
Your Vote and How to Use It is a civics handbook by Mrs Raymond Brown, chairman of organization of the New York State Woman Suffrage Party. Harper published it in February 1918, with a foreword by Carrie Chapman Catt, president of the National American Woman Suffrage Association. The book is officially endorsed by the New York State Woman Suffrage Party. It is dedicated to the many good citizens who helped prepare it.

The chapters begin with Politics and Woman's Interests: the duties of government and its relation to the home. Town and county government follow, with the town meeting and the kind of men needed as officials. Village and city government come next, with classes of charters and wards. A chapter survey preserved in the copy reaches Greater New York itself.
70651-passion-fruit:
H De Vere Stacpoole wrote a tale billed as a grim chapter from the South Seas, in which Carstairs loves and forgets while the girl never does. The scene is New Caledonia, seen from a ship coming up from Sydney or Brisbane. Coral reef, gulls, and highlands rise beyond, with a white lighthouse marking the entry to Noumea harbor.

France long sent convicts to this paradise, and their passions remain after the shipments stopped. Monsieur Roche, a restaurant keeper, tells the narrator strange stories. His own father, a clock maker, was deported for making clockwork for a bomb. He points out Marianne Ribot, a woman of faded beauty in yellow and black.
71166-wisdom-while-you-wait:
Wisdom While You Wait, printed for private circulation in 1902, spoofs a grand new paper whose name is a mouthful of coined syllables. Fake ads lead off: Pierpont's Soap, which defies rivals, knocks spots off the leopard, and makes the stars white, with a testimonial from a magnate who cries, what a soap. Pale pills for pink people follow.

Mock mastheads list editors by department in jest: one man for obituaries, one for Napoleon, one for tobacco, one for trusts, and Sousa for music. Names of press lords, royals, and show folk are bandied for sport. The booklet is Edwardian insider humor, a foretaste of glories promised by a paper that never was, full of puns and trade slang.
71997-from-ploughshare-to-pulpit:
From Ploughshare to Pulpit, a tale of the battle of life by Gordon Stables, a Royal Navy surgeon, reached a second edition in London. Stables wrote The Cruise of the Snowbird and Children of the Mountain. A verse line on the title page praises a man who walked in glory following his plough on a mountainside. The book is dedicated to his old Aberdeen professor.

Three books trace a ploughman student from the old farm of Kilbuie to college and then far at sea. Chapters promise a bully smashed, a ball, a storm ride on snowshoes, town and gown fights, and hard study. Faith, grit, and love carry the hero from farm work toward the pulpit.
72249-through-time-and-space-with-benedi:
Through Time and Space with Benedict Breadfruit is a set of short science fiction sketches by Grandall Barretton. They ran in Amazing Stories from March to October 1962. Each piece is a small numbered episode, signed by the author. Benedict Breadfruit travels the planets solving problems in a line or two.

On Phogiu the Second, a huge intelligent lichen, the local god, is dying. Breadfruit gives it a vitamin shot and a chlorophyll pill. The lichen perks up and resumes its deep pronouncements. The trouble was only a weak algae part, needing a buttress. Other sketches treat space lice removed by gas, and a battered robot. Barretton's humour runs dry and quick.
72518-the-minister-had-to-wait:
Roger Dee placed a science fiction tale in the June-July 1953 issue of Fantastic Universe. Doc Maxey has built a tube that cuts through the dimensions of space. He swears he did not build it as a weapon and will not see it made one.

The brass come to his Connecticut laboratory to take it by force of law. A state of world emergency has been declared, they say. Both halves of the globe sit roofed by force screens that blunt atomic bombs, and the power those screens eat is draining both sides dry. The tube could send warheads through the screens by a short cut in space. The generals talk of ants and sheets of paper. Maxey calls their talk childish, borrowed from the comic tapes, and stalks out, till a guard's rifle brings him back.
72906-the-way-of-the-spirit:
The Way of the Spirit is a novel by H Rider Haggard, published in London in nineteen hundred six. Scripture mottoes on youth, judgment, and the tree of life head the title page. Haggard dedicates the book to his dear Kipling in a long letter. Both men believe there are higher aims in life than weaving stories, that letter states.

Kipling had talked over the plan of the tale with Haggard and read the written book, the dedication adds. His judgment of it pleased its author enough to print. Spirit, faith, and adventure meet in a tale planned between the two great romancers of empire. Haggard steps beyond lost cities toward the life of the soul.
7293-the-opium-habit:
The Opium Habit gathers accounts of addiction and attempts at cure. It opens with Coleridge's earnest plea that after his death a full narrative of his wretchedness and its guilty cause be made public. He hoped some little good might come from the direful example. Its contents move from a successful attempt to abandon opium through De Quincey's Confessions and Coleridge's own reminiscences to William Blair and the comparison of opium and alcohol.

Insanity and suicide, a morphine habit overcome, and the cases of Robert Hall, John Randolph, and William Wilberforce follow, closing with outlines of the opium cure. The book mixes confession, case history, and moral warning in a Victorian voice. It reads as both testimony and tract against a spreading habit.
73651-modern-shipbuilding-and-the-men-en:
Modern Shipbuilding and the Men Engaged in It is a survey by David Pollock, a naval architect, printed at London in 1884. Its subtitle promises a review of recent progress in steamship design and construction. It adds descriptions of notable shipyards and statistics of work done in the principal building districts. Portraits and biographical notes of eminent shipowners, shipbuilders, engineers, and naval architects go with the text.

In his preface Pollock notes the great activity in shipbuilding and marine engineering in recent years. The substantial progress in science and practice, he says, has filled the technical and daily press. Yet no single work, so far as he knows, has dealt historically with modern shipbuilding in a way at once trustworthy and popular. A plate shows the steamship City of Rome of the Anchor Line.
74226-horsesense-hank-does-his-bit:
Nelson Bond wrote this comic war tale for Amazing Stories, where it ran in May 1942. Pearl Harbor made Horsesense Hank mad, the head note says. Something ought to be done, and Hank was the man to do it.

The narrator had just fixed all things smooth at Midland U, his old school. He had got his friend Hank Cleaver engaged to Helen MacDowell. Then That Man stepped in: Hitler, the ex-housepainter with the scrap of brush on his lip. The narrator reels off the lands seized, from Austria to Greece and Crete. Hank, a campus fool with a good heart, will now do his bit in the war in his own mad way.
74651-frank-hardy-s-choice-and-what-came:
Frank Hardy's Choice, by O'Brien, is a tale for boys printed in London and Edinburgh. Eight short chapters make up the main story. Two lads talk at a road corner in Springcliffe, a small seaside village. Frank Hardy, aged sixteen, refuses to join evening school. Classes run three nights a week after work ends at six. He calls that a theft of spare time and stands for liberty.

Walter, his younger friend, defends his mother's counsel. Tom Haines, an older youth, whispers a secret plan to Frank. Chapter heads promise right and wrong, unjust suspicions, and poachers. A plate shows a pheasant's tail feather by moonlight. The tale weighs ease and bad company against duty, in a plain moral frame.
75599-the-truth-about-the-tobacco-habit:
The Truth About the Tobacco Habit is a pamphlet by T. Swann Harding, issued as Little Blue Book number 1389 by the Haldeman-Julius company of Girard, Kansas. The editor of the series is named on the title page. The booklet was copyrighted in 1929.

Harding opens with stories, not statistics. A young smoker with a stomach pain is told by his doctor to quit, is threatened with an operation, and recovers only when he drops buckwheat cakes and sausage from his diet. A second friend gets the same treatment in reverse. The tales set up the book's sceptical question. How much of the blame laid on tobacco rests on habit and guesswork rather than proof? The hosted text comes from Project Gutenberg.
76083-pursuit:
Andrew A. Caffrey wrote this tale of the men of the air in the Great War. Its head note names it a tale of the Balloon Strafers of America. When the chiefs split Jack Langdon from his group of chase planes, the note says, they came close to the break of a stout heart of flight. Langdon was sent to fly the two-seat planes, the slow scouts of the sky. For him there was no choice but to pack and go.

A plea would have got him naught, and would have been bad form to boot. Still, twixt high rage and low soul, the boy hung and pined for days. To fly chase, to hunt in the air, was the sum of all that war could give. To drive a two-seat plane was plain hell in his eyes.
76260-hand-made-furniture-and-how-to-mak:
Hand Made Furniture and How to Make It, by Albert Glidden of the Hand Made Furniture Shop in Spokane, was copyrighted in 1910. Glidden aims the book at readers who want a pleasant, paying craft, or furniture for their homes that shows their own taste: sturdy honesty of purpose, simple beauty, comfort, and durability.

Early chapters teach tools one by one: the saw, plane, chisels, marking gauge, brace and bits, hammer, and squares, with sharpening and use. Later chapters cover squaring and jointing, mortise and tenon work, dovetailing, panelling, staining, dyeing, filling, and polishing. Closing designs give a piano bench, plant stand, music cabinet, hall seat, hat tree, dining table, chairs, and a library table, all in the plain mission manner of the day.
76619-hetty-s-garden-party-and-what-came:
Emma Leslie wrote Hetty’s Garden-Party, and What Came of It, a tale for young readers. The Sunday School Union issued the book in London from Old Bailey. Leslie had written Harry Lawley and Constancia’s Household before. Six chapters tell the whole of Hetty Golding’s small trial.

A letter from Uncle John starts the tale at breakfast. Cousins Harry and Lettice will come for a week’s stay. Hetty claps her hands and plans a fine show at once. Her widowed mother keeps one servant on a tight purse. Uncle John keeps two, plus cook and kitchen maid. Hetty has puffed her home’s wealth to the girls near by. Now the lean truth must face her rich kin at her own table. Pride, a dilemma, and an unwelcome guest fill the short tale.
778-five-children-and-it:
E. Nesbit sends five children, Robert, Anthea, Cyril, Jane, and the Lamb, to a house in the country. There they dig up a Psammead, a grumpy sand fairy who grants one wish a day. Each wish goes wrong in a funny, instructive way. Nesbit wrote Five Children and It in 1902, founding a new kind of children's fantasy.

Wishes for beauty, wealth, wings, and grown-up size bring trouble that lasts till sunset, when the magic fades. Nesbit writes with wit and warmth, and the book founded the modern children's fantasy of everyday magic. The Psammead, grumpy and ancient, became a model for later magical creatures in children's books.
78154-art-and-the-human-spirit:
Edward Howard Griggs gave these eight lectures on art and the human spirit, and Huebsch printed the handbook at New York in 1908. The subtitle names his ground: the meaning and ties of sculpture, painting, poetry, and music. A creed in praise of art heads the book.

The creed, set down by a famed hand of the past, trusts in God, Mozart, and Beethoven. It calls art one and whole, sent from God and lodged in bright hearts. It blesses those who hunger for art's sake and damns those who trade on it for gain. Griggs builds his lectures on that faith, treating the four arts as one speech of the soul.
79640-myra-sherwood-s-cross-and-how-she-:
Myra Sherwood's Cross and How She Bore It, by Lucy Ellen Guernsey, author of The Object of Life, was published in London by the Religious Tract Society. Twenty chapters trace Myra from childhood incidents and a family history to the last of the story. A front plate shows riders galloping off for their lives. Trials of principle, secrets, and sorrow fill the heads.

The tale opens as a lady holds a newborn whose mother has just been laid in the family vault. The grandfather, mourning his lost daughter, names the baby Myra and bids that she be raised to match her mother, whose picture shall hang in the nursery. Later chapters bring Harry's lessons and adventures afar, sisters' love, and lessons in the school of Christ. Guernsey writes a firm, tender tale of faith under grief.
8904-how-to-do-it:
Edward Everett Hale collects papers on how young people succeed or fail in How To Do It. Opening with how we met and moving through how to talk, how to write, how to read in two chapters. How to go into society. Life at school, life in vacation, life alone, habits in church, life with children, life with elders, habits of reading, and getting ready complete the course. Hale says the papers enter into detail about many young people of his acquaintance, named only in disguise.

Hale, Boston minister and author, writes as a friendly mentor, practical rather than preachy, about manners, study, and character. The book captures Gilded Age advice for youth: talk well, read well, behave well, and use time well. Modern readers will find some counsel dated and some timeless, and a charming window onto what earnest adults once thought young people most needed to learn.
963-little-dorrit:
Charles Dickens sets Little Dorrit in the Marshalsea debtors' prison, where Amy Dorrit was born and where her father, the Father of the Marshalsea, holds court. Book One is called Poverty, and Book Two, Riches. Dickens published Little Dorrit in parts from 1855 to 1857, as a darker late novel.

Amy's quiet goodness meets Arthur Clennam's search for a family secret, while Mr. Merdle's fraud and the Circumlocution Office satirise a whole society. The novel is one of Dickens's darkest and most mature works. The Marshalsea, where Dickens's own father had been jailed for debt, gives the book its pain.
968-martin-chuzzlewit:
Charles Dickens wrote this novel about Martin Chuzzlewit, young and old, and the family greed that surrounds them. Young Martin, proud and selfish, quarrels with his grandfather, falls under the oily Mr. Pecksniff, and sails to America, where Eden, a swampy settlement, teaches him hard lessons about himself.

Dickens satirises America, insurance fraud, and hypocrisy with great vigour, while Martin learns humility and love. Mrs. Gamp, the nurse, and Mr. Pecksniff are among his finest comic creations. Martin Chuzzlewit stands as a rich, sprawling Dickens novel, and a turning point in his art toward darker comedy.
9864-humoresque-a-laugh-on-life-with-a-t:
Fannie Hurst wrote Humoresque in 1920, stories of New York's immigrant streets, laughing on the surface with tears behind. The title tale opens on the Bowery, where seventeen languages steam from tenements, pushcarts, and clotheslines. Mulberry Street runs its Latin length of vermicelli, rhinestone combs, and naked babies. A fiddler capers through Dvorak's melody, ironic as a grinning mask.

Other stories include Oats for the Woman, A Petal on the Current, and White Goods, with heads, boobs, and wrong pews beside. Hurst writes with lush, humane color. A reader gets a vivid set of immigrant tales, where humor and heartbreak share one street.
abbeychurch-or-self-control-and-self-con:
Charlotte M. Yonge's Abbeychurch, her first novel, is presented in this second edition with a preface calling it her first crude attempt. The epigraph is Newman's warning: never think yourself safe for doing your duty in ninety-nine points; the hundredth is the ground of self-denial. The subtitle names the two diseases, Self-Control and Self-Conceit, set against each other in a town where the abbey church is to be restored. Yonge's young authorial voice already has its program: parish life as the theater of the soul.

Inside, two heroines carry the contrast, one governing herself into stiffness, one mistaking her own opinions for conscience. The clergyman must learn to direct, not obstruct, the march of improvement. Readers meeting Yonge at her beginning get the seed of the Victorian domestic novel's Tractarian branch: a restoration quarrel in stone that is really about who owns a parish's soul.
an-essay-on-comedy-and-the-uses-of-the-c:
George Meredith first published his essay on comedy in the New Quarterly Magazine for April 1877, as this 1897 printing notes. He asks what true comedy is and what good it does. For Meredith, the comic spirit watches human folly with a clear eye and corrects it by laughter rather than by preaching.

He argues that fine comedy needs a society of quick, cultivated minds, and that women must stand as equals in it, or the comic sense stays crude. Molière stands as his model, with Shakespeare and the Greeks behind. The essay is dense and demanding, but it shaped how later critics talk about comedy's social work.
an-introductory-course-of-quantitative-c: Henry Paul Talbot offers an introductory course of quantitative chemical analysis, with explanatory notes for students. The book teaches the measurement of substances by careful weighing and titration, with methods set out step by step. Talbot's course served as a laboratory standard for beginners in chemistry. Clear tables and worked cases aid the new student.
as-you-like-it:
William Shakespeare's As You Like It, in the old-spelling text of this electronic set, sends Rosalind and Orlando into the Forest of Arden. The notes prefacing the file explain the printers' swapped letters across the set, Hamlet examples included. Banished by Duke Frederick, Rosalind disguises herself as the youth Ganymede.

Orlando hangs verses on the trees, berimed like Pythagoras's transmigrated soul, Rosalind jokes, and she schools him in love while pretending to be a man. Phebe's scornful letter to the shepherd Silvius shows the comedy's other register. Jaques's seven ages speech crowns the pastoral. Shakespeare's sunniest comedy ends with four marriages and Hymen's blessing, its wit carried by the greatest heroine he ever wrote.
britannica-1911-abu-hanifa-an-nu-man-ibn:
Abu Hanifa an-Nu'man ibn Thabit (699-767) was a Muslim canon lawyer of Kufa, born of non-Arab, probably Persian, parentage. A silk dealer with means of his own, he could give his time to legal study. He lectured on fiqh, Islamic law, and advised as a mufti, a jurist who gives legal opinions, while refusing public office.

Office was pressed on him anyway. The caliph al-Mansur made him an overseer of craftsmen while Baghdad was built, and wanted him as a judge, which he resisted. Reports differ, but imprisonment and beating for that refusal seem certain. His tomb in eastern Baghdad still stood when the entry was written, and his school shaped Muslim law.
britannica-1911-affidavit:
Affidavit, a Latin based word for he has declared upon oath, is defined in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It is a written statement sworn or affirmed before a person who may give an oath. Proof is chiefly taken this way in the Chancery Division of the High Court in England. Such proof serves on a petition, summons, or motion.

Steps taken before trial also run on affidavits, as for the showing of papers. That set is called an affidavit of documents by lawyers. Affidavits can also serve as proof that set forms were duly done, such as the service of court papers. They see wide use in bankruptcy work, in tax work, and in lower courts. In will cases, all papers such as wills and drafts must be filed in this sworn form.
britannica-1911-agathodaemon-spirit: Agathodaemon, in Greek myth, is the subject of a brief entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was the good spirit of cornfields and vineyards. Greeks drank a cup of pure wine in his honour at the end of each meal. He was also seen as a guard spirit of the state and of each person, often paired with Good Fortune.
britannica-1911-algae-habit:
Habit, a section of the Algae article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica, surveys the shapes algae take. Surveying the whole range, Oltmanns distinguishes bush-forms, whip forms, net-forms, leaf-forms, sack-forms, forms flattened back-to-belly, and cushions, plates, and crusts. Many algae bear leaf-like branches of limited growth, and herbarium specimens often strike viewers by their likeness to trees and shrubs.

Cladophora and Bryopsis show the bushy pattern, while Spirogyra and Chorda are whip-forms and Hydrodictyon a true net-form. Leaf-forms are the most varied, since a large surface exposed to light is a clear advantage. Some, such as Delesseria, carry a strengthening midrib and rich veining, making the likeness to a flowering plant's leaf striking. Others, including Agarum and Claudea, are leaf-forms perforated with holes. Enteromorpha stands for the sack-forms, a hollow tube of green tissue.
britannica-1911-auber-daniel-francois-es:
Daniel François Esprit Auber, French composer born at Caen in Normandy on 29 January 1782, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was the son of a Paris print seller. His father meant him for trade in life. Yet the boy was let to follow his love of music and learned several instruments at an early age.

A Tirolean composer was his first teacher in the art. At age twenty he was sent to London to finish his training for business. The breach of the treaty of Amiens in 1804 forced him to leave England in haste. He had by then tried his hand at writing music for the stage and the hall. Praise for a violin concerto played at the Conservatoire spurred him to reset an old comic opera. Aware of his gaps, he then sought full study of his chosen art.
britannica-1911-belit:
Belit, a name meaning “the lady” above all others, was in Babylonian religion the wife of the god Bel. Her own name was Nin-lil, “lady of power,” and she was also called Nin-Khar-sag, “Lady of the mountain.” That title links her to the sacred tower of Bel at Nippur.

As wife of En-lil, Belit belonged to Nippur and bore grand titles like “ruler of heaven and earth” and “mother of the gods.” Kings honoured her with offerings and fortresses, yet like most Babylonian goddesses she stood in her husband’s shadow. Later the name Belit passed to Ishtar, and also to Sarpanit, wife of Marduk.
britannica-1911-beloit:
Beloit is a city of Rock county, Wisconsin, on the state’s south border where the Rock river runs. It lies ninety-one miles north-west of Chicago and counted 6,315 people in 1890, rising to 15,125 by 1910. Two railways and an interurban electric line serve the city, set on high bluffs above the river.

Beloit College, founded in 1847 under Congregational and Presbyterian care, teaches men and women together and runs classical, philosophical and scientific courses. River power drives mills making ploughs, steam pumps, windmills, paper machinery, cutlery and flour, and factory output topped four million dollars in 1905. New Englanders founded the place in 1838, and it took a city charter in 1856.
britannica-1911-bering-island-sea-and-st:
Bering Island, Bering Sea and Bering Strait all take their name from the explorer Vitus Bering. The island, where he died, lies off Kamchatka in the sea’s south-west, one of Russia’s Commander group. It runs sixty-nine miles long, rises only about three hundred feet, and holds some 650 people on a treeless shore in a severe climate.

Bering Sea is the Pacific’s northward reach, fenced by the Aleutian chain, Alaska to the east and Siberia west, covering about 870,000 square miles. Its seal fisheries are a great prize. Bering Strait joins it to the Arctic Ocean, where Asia’s East Cape comes within about fifty-six miles of Cape Prince of Wales in America. Cook’s voyage of 1778 opened these waters fully to the world.
britannica-1911-biscuit:
Biscuit is a form of bread baked in thin, crisp cakes, from the French for twice-cooked. The Latin parts are bis, twice, and coctum, cooked, a nod to its first making. In the United States such goods are usually called crackers instead. The word biscuit there, and in northern England, means small raised loaves. Unglazed earthenware after its first firing is also called biscuit, or bisque. The 1911 Britannica article is a full trade treatment of the baked kind.

Flour is the chief raw material, with butter, sugar, salt, and flavourings in support. Biscuit flour differs from bread flour, wanting less strength and water uptake. The article follows mixing, rolling, cutting, and baking step by step. Fancy kinds are glazed by spraying them with fine jets of fresh milk. Cracknels, made from very stiff dough, are boiled before they meet a fierce oven. Zimmer signs the long, practical piece.
britannica-1911-circuit:
Circuit is a word for the act of going round, from Latin roots for round and to go. It names a circumference, or a thing that rings or is ringed. The word is best known as a term of law. There it names the set progress of a court through the provinces of a land to do the work of the law. It has long named the trips of judges through the counties of England to hold courts.
