In England the Judicature Act of 1875 gave the crown power to make rules about circuits by order in council. Those rules can end a circuit, form a new one, and fix the place where assizes are to be held. An order of 5 February 1876 was made under that power. The article goes on to set out how the system of circuits then stood.
britannica-1911-cockpit: Cockpit first meant an enclosed place where cock fighting was held as sport. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica traces how the name spread to other uses in London. Offices for the treasury and privy council kept the old name for years. A London theatre built on the Drury Lane site also bore it. On warships the word named a lower deck cabin. Wounded men were tended there in battle, and junior officers gathered there as well.
britannica-1911-credit:
Credit, from the Latin credere, to believe, means belief or trust in its general sense. The word also covers the repute a person holds and the esteem in which others hold him. In commerce it means a promise to pay at a future time for value received in the present. A good name for meeting such promises is itself called credit. In book-keeping, credit is the side of an account where payments are entered.

From that book-keeping sense, the word sometimes stands for the payments themselves. The entry leaves the wider role of credit in trade to the economic text-books. It points readers to Knies on money and credit and to Macleod's Theory of Credit. It also cites Hartley Withers and his book The Meaning of Money, published in 1909. The whole entry is a compact account of the word's senses, from trust to ledger practice.
britannica-1911-cuckoo-spit: Cuckoo-spit is the frothy matter found upon plants in gardens and fields. The hosted entry, a short note, states that the froth is made by the young, nymph stage of various plant-lice. Those insects belong to the families Cercopidae and Jassidae, in the homopterous division of the Hemiptera. In their grown state the same insects are sometimes called frog-hoppers. The entry gives no account of how the froth is formed or why.
britannica-1911-culprit:
Culprit properly names the prisoner at the bar, one accused of a crime, and by extension anyone guilty of an offence. Its origin is a pairing of two Anglo-French law words. Culpable meant guilty, and prit, or prist, meant ready. When a prisoner pleaded not guilty, the clerk of the crown answered culpable and said he was ready to join issue. The words cul. prist were then written on the roll.

When French law terms fell away, the two words were misread as one word spoken to the prisoner. The formula, Culprit, how will you be tried, first appears in the trial of the 7th earl of Pembroke for murder in 1678. That courtroom scene fixed the word in English. A note in a roll thus became the everyday name for an accused or guilty person. The entry gives no wider use beyond that legal birth.
britannica-1911-elegit:
Elegit is an old writ in English law, explained in a short 1911 Britannica entry on court process. The Latin name means he has chosen, from words in the writ itself. The writ came from the Statute of Westminster the Second in 1285. Before that law, a creditor who won in court could take only the gains from land, not the land.

The statute let the winner choose a writ against goods and half the land of the debtor. That right held until the debt was paid in full. Since the Bankruptcy Act of 1883 the writ reached land and houses alone. The entry points readers on to the wider topic of execution for more detail.
britannica-1911-fit:
Fit is a word with several meanings, and a short word study in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica takes them in turn. In one sense a fit is a part or division of a poem, a canto. In that sense the word is often spelled fytte. In a second sense it names a sudden attack of illness.

That attack is brief, and it may come with convulsions and a loss of sense. The entry ties the word above all to apoplexy and epilepsy. It is also used of passing attacks of gout, of coughing, and of fainting. By transfer it covers bursts of tears, of mirth, or of temper. Hence comes the phrase by fits and starts. As an adjective, fit means suitable or proper. It often carries the sense of having the needed powers for a set task.
britannica-1911-flechier-esprit:
Esprit Flechier (1632-1710), French preacher and author, bishop of Nimes, was born at Pernes in Vaucluse on 10 June 1632. His uncle, head of the Doctrinaires, raised him at Tarascon, and Flechier entered that order. On his uncle's death he left it, finding its rules too strict, and went to Paris to write poetry. His French poems won little, but a Latin verse account of a tournament given by Louis XIV in 1662 made his reputation.

Flechier tutored a future finance chief and went with him to Clermont, where he wrote his curious Memoirs of the Grands Jours, a half-romantic record of that extraordinary court. In 1668 he became reader to the dauphin, and his sermons grew famous. The entry, whose closing pages open the hosted Fleet file, praises his wit, ingenuity and harmony of diction, while noting a love of symmetry and antithesis. His histories of Theodosius and of Ximenes close the account.
britannica-1911-godwit:
Godwit is the name of a marsh bird once prized for the table and common in the fens of Norfolk and Lincolnshire. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica gathers old praise for it: in 1544 it cost three times a snipe, and later writers kept its fame alive. Two British kinds went under the one name.

The bird most prized is the black-tailed godwit, once nicknamed yarwhelp or shrieker for its loud cry. Netting in spring and summer, with the draining of the fens, drove it from breeding in England by about 1824. It still ranges wide, summering as far as Iceland and wintering in India. The bar-tailed godwit only passes through Britain in May, breeds in Lapland, and lays eggs so rare that few have seen them. Both kinds are pigeon-sized, with long legs and a long bill that turns slightly up.
britannica-1911-hit:
Hit is a town of Asiatic Turkey in the province of Baghdad. The 1911 Britannica entry sets it on the west bank of the Euphrates. It lies 70 miles west north west of Baghdad on the river. The town perches on a line of hills by the water side. Those hills are in large part heaps of old town waste.

Houses there are built of field stones and of mud in the main. A tall minaret leans at a clear slant and draws the eye. Behind the town spreads a wide plain, bare and stark in view. Streams of bitter water flow there from mineral springs in the ground. Two bitumen springs, one cold and one hot, lie close by town.
britannica-1911-letter-of-credit: Letter of Credit is a short trade entry in the 1911 Britannica. It is a letter from a banker or a merchant. It asks a second man or firm for an advance. The advance goes to the bearer or a named man. It is made on the credit of the man who wrote it. Such a letter is general or special in its kind. A general one speaks to merchants at large for aid. A special one names one man to make the advance.
britannica-1911-millstone-grit:
Millstone Grit, in earth science a set of thick sandstones and shales, is described in a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry. The set rests right on the Carboniferous Limestone, or on shales that sit between. Thin coal seams in it show that coal forming had begun.

Its outcrop runs from the Bristol coal field through Wales to the north midland counties. It is fullest there and in Lancashire and Yorkshire, then runs on to Scotland. The grits are of one broad type but vary from place to place. They look like sand banks formed as the old sea grew shallow. In Lancashire the set is said to be five thousand feet thick. Named grit layers are listed in order.
britannica-1911-orbit:
Orbit, from a Latin word for a track, is defined in a star science entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It is the path of a body as it circles a centre that draws it. Under the pull of gravity, that path takes the shape of a conic section, an ellipse, a parabola or a hyperbola.

The centre of pull sits at one focus of the curve, and the motion follows the laws of Kepler. A body on a path that is not an ellipse will never come round again. So the entry keeps its focus on the ellipse, with the parabola as a limiting case. Other forces can bend the path away from a true conic, even into a chain of spires. In practice such forces are so small that the orbit stays near an ellipse, and the maths can start from there.
britannica-1911-peter-the-hermit:
Peter the Hermit was a priest of Amiens who preached the first crusade, as the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica tells. He may have tried a pilgrimage to Jerusalem before 1096 and been kept from his goal by the Turks. It is unsure if he heard the great sermon of Urban at Clermont in 1095. He was one of the preachers of the crusade in France after it.

He leapt to fame as a preacher who could stir a crowd to tears. His very ass was held as a holy thing by the folk. Thousands of peasants took the cross at his word. The crusade of the poor folk was his work, and he led one of its five bands to Constantinople in 1096. There his host, which had made a pest of itself by theft, crossed to the Asian shore.
britannica-1911-pipit:
Pipit is the subject of a bird article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Pipits are a group of birds much like larks in habits and look. They differ from larks in several key traits. Bird scholars now place them with the wagtails in one family. Over fifty species have been described across the world. North America holds only two species of the group.

The article says the best known species to English readers is the meadow pipit. That bird abounds on pastures, moors, and wild ground. In some places the tree pipit takes its place. It draws notice by its loud song, delivered on the wing in a short circling flight. A third species, the rock pipit, scarcely ever leaves the sea coast. It is found almost all round the British Isles. A South African group with a very long hind claw is also placed among the pipits.
britannica-1911-prakrit:
Prakrit is a language article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about the common tongues of India. The word means natural, and it stands against Sanskrit, which means purified. Sanskrit was the fixed tongue of books, while the Prakrits were the speech of daily life.

The article sorts the old tongues into two main groups. One group held the midland of India, and its speech hardened into book Sanskrit. The rest kept changing as spoken tongues do. In time some of those tongues won books of their own. One became Pali, the holy tongue of Buddhism. Others served the Jain faith and the stage. In Indian plays, high folk speak Sanskrit on stage. The rest speak a Prakrit fitted to their land and trade.
britannica-1911-pulpit:
Pulpit, from a Latin word for a stage or platform, is the subject of an entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. A pulpit is a raised stand with a closed front, from which sermons are given. Its modern form most likely grew out of the ambones of the early Christian church. Many old pulpits are of stone, though most are of wood.

Church pulpits are most often six or eight sided, set on stone bases or slim wooden stems. Their carving, panels, and ornament follow the style of their age, and some are rich with colour and gilding. A canopy or sounding board tops a few of them. The usual place is in the nave, on the north side. Outdoor pulpits, for speaking to crowds in the open air, were common in medieval times.
britannica-1911-smith-gerrit:
Gerrit Smith, American reformer and giver of vast sums, was born in Utica in New York on 6 March 1797 and is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. After graduation at Hamilton College in 1818, he took charge of the vast estate of his father. Peter Smith had long been a partner of John Jacob Astor in trade. Gerrit Smith greatly increased the family fortune in his care.

At about 1828 he became an active worker in the cause of temperance. In his home village of Peterboro he built one of the first temperance hotels in the country. He became an abolitionist in 1835 after he saw a mob break up an anti slavery meeting at Utica. In 1840 he took a leading part in founding the Liberty party for that cause. Its remnant named him for the presidency in 1848 and again in 1852.
britannica-1911-soyer-alexis-benoit:
Alexis Benoît Soyer was a French cook of great fame, born at Meaux-en-Brie in France, as this 1911 Britannica article tells. After five years learning the trade near Versailles, he became chief cook for a well known Paris eating house. He left France at the uprising of 1830 and went to London, where he cooked for nobles and, from 1837, for the Reform Club.

In 1847 the state sent him to set up kitchens in Dublin during the famine in Ireland. In 1855 he went at his own cost to the Crimea to advise on cooking for the British army there. On his return he helped reform the food of army hospitals. He invented an army cooking wagon and wrote a range of cookery books, and died in London in 1858.
britannica-1911-summit:
Summit, a city in Union County, New Jersey, is the subject of a 1911 Britannica place entry. It sits on the crest of a ridge called Second Mountain, west of New York City. Its mean height is four hundred fifty feet. Rail lines link it to New York and to towns in its own state. Its folk count reached seven thousand five hundred in nineteen ten, with growth at each count.

Home life for New York workers is its chief draw, with summer guests as well. A town book hall dates from eighteen seventy four. A home for blind children, a care house, and a school for girls serve the town. A stone on Hobart Hill marks a war time beacon and signal gun post. Town rule dates from eighteen sixty nine.
britannica-1911-whitebait:
Whitebait is the common name for small fish that crowd into the Thames estuary each summer, and a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry traces how the name was sorted out. The fish was prized as a treat for the table. Early writers took it to be a species of its own. Some linked it to the bleak, and one writer called it the young of the shad.

Work by W. Yarrell in 1820 showed that the shad claim rested on wrong samples. Yet Yarrell still listed the fish as its own kind, under the name Clupea alba. Later study showed whitebait is in fact the young fry of herring and kin. The entry gives readers a neat case of how close checks can fix a long held error.
britannica-1911-writ:
Writ, in law, is a formal order from the crown or an officer acting for it, telling someone to do or not do some act. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article traces the word from the Latin breve, so called because it states its maker's meaning in few words. Traces reach back to the Roman writer Paulus, around the year 220.

Kindred forms turn up in feudal law, where the sealed note of a land grant grew into the deed. In church law a papal breve was less formal than a bull. In England the writ became the base of all pleading in the king's court. By the reign of Henry the Second the forms were fixed, and Glanvill's book gives early patterns. Writs arose as cases demanded, not from any set plan, and their fees long fed the exchequer.
bumper-the-white-rabbit:
George Ethelbert Walsh wrote a set of tales of a white rabbit, Bumper, for the Twilight Animal Series. Edwin John Prittie drew the colour plates. John C. Winston put out the book at Chicago, Philadelphia, and Toronto. A run of short stories, each a step in Bumper's road, fills the frame.

Where Bumper came from opens the set. Why he was left at home and how he was sold come next. A dread house, a red-haired girl, and Carlo the dog mark the early turns. Sewer rat, bat nest, and a raft flight raise the stakes. First black crow and a fox test him in the mid-run. Walsh's own list shows a string of Bumper books — in the woods, with foes, with friends — so this set starts a long line. Small size and white fur set Bumper apart in each scrape.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-augustine-fra:
Augustine Francis Hewit was a priest and second Superior General of the Paulists, born at Fairfield, Connecticut, in 1820, who died in New York in 1897. His father was a prominent Congregational minister, and his mother was a senator's daughter. Schooled at Fairfield, Andover, and Amherst, he balked at his parents' Calvinist tenets, studied at the East Windsor seminary, and was licensed to preach. Convinced that episcopacy, rule by bishops, is of divine origin, he joined the Episcopal Church.

He took Anglican deacon's orders in 1844, under Tract 90's reading of the Thirty-nine Articles, and followed the Oxford Movement ardently. Newman's conversion in 1845 unsettled him, and he submitted to the Catholic Church on 25 March 1846. Under his later lead, the Paulists ran the first regular missions for non-Catholics in America. They founded a house at San Francisco and opened St Thomas College at the Catholic University in Washington in 1889.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cardinal-deus:
Deusdedit was an eleventh-century cardinal born at Todi who died between 1097 and 1100. A Benedictine and friend of Gregory VII, he championed that pope's reforms and rose to the cardinalate with the title of St. Peter in Chains. He took part in a Roman synod in 1078, speaking for the views of Berengarius of Tours, and stood among Gregory's chief agents against civil oppression of church authority.

At Gregory's suggestion he compiled a collection of canons, finished in 1087 and dedicated to Victor III. Its four books run to 327 chapters on the Roman Church's power, 163 on the Roman clergy, 289 on church matters, and 437 on the liberty of the Church. The entry also notes a German sojourn known only from a chapter heading, with its date and motive unrecorded.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-habit:
Habit, the effect of repeated acts and the readiness to repeat them, is examined here as both a fact of life and a question for philosophy and theology. The entry defines it, after Rickaby, as a quality hard to change that disposes an agent to follow one line of action easily and at will. Its marks are regularity, quickness, less effort, and a drift toward automatic action.

Seven sections carry the treatment through general, bodily, mental, moral, educational, philosophical, and theological aspects. Repetition strengthens the trace left by each act, and habit branches into neighbouring actions and roots itself deeper. Without it even dressing, eating, and walking would demand fresh effort at every step, which is why habit has been called a second nature.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-introit:
The entrance chant of the Mass, a psalm fragment with its antiphon sung as priest and ministers walk to the altar, is the subject of this liturgy entry. Every Western rite began Mass with such a processional psalm from the earliest times on record. Choirs sang it, so it appears not in sacramentaries but in the oldest antiphonaries, including the Gregorian book at Montpellier and the St Gall manuscript of seventh-century tradition.

A Roman order from the sixth or seventh century pictures the scene. Candles are lit. Singers stand before the altar on either side. The choir leader starts the entrance antiphon. Deacons fetch the pope from the sacristy at the sound of his voice. The entry thus recovers the sound and staging of the Mass's first moments in the early Church.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-louis-gallait:
Louis Gallait was a Flemish painter, born at Tournai in 1810 and dead at Brussels in 1887. His pictures run to the melodramatic and pathetic, in the manner of Ary Scheffer, yet with stronger colour and surer drawing, and a like devotional, sentimental fire.

A child prodigy, he painted his first picture at ten and won a local prize. Tournai's gift sent him to Paris in 1835 to study under Hennequin, and honours followed: the Institute of France, honorary Royal Academician, and shows in London in 1862 and 1872. He worked in oil and watercolour alike, and his emotional history scenes won a wide public.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-merit:
Merit, in general, means that quality of a good work which entitles its doer to a reward from the one in whose service the work is done. By extension the word also names the good work itself, insofar as it deserves a reward from the person served. In theology, a supernatural merit can only be a salutary act, to which God, by his unfailing promise, owes a supernatural reward, ultimately eternal life, the beatific vision in heaven.

The entry's main aim is to defend the Catholic doctrine that good works merit reward. It proceeds under four heads: nature of merit, existence of merit, conditions of merit, and objects of merit. On nature, only positively good works can bear merit. Bad works, whether they help or hurt a third party, hold nothing but demerit and deserve punishment. The good workman deserves his labour's reward, and the thief deserves his crime's punishment.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-michel-benoit:
Michel Benoit, born at Autun or Dijon on 8 October 1715, died at Peking on 23 October 1774: a Jesuit scientist who served China's Kien Lung emperor for thirty years. He studied at Dijon and St. Sulpice, Paris, and entered the Nancy Jesuit novitiate in 1737. After three years of renewed pleas, he won his wish for the China mission, but first finished astronomical studies at Paris under de l'Isle, de la Caille, and Le Monnier.

Reaching Peking in 1744 or 1745 amid a provincial persecution of missionaries, Benoit was kept at court, since the government's need of science made missionaries indispensable. He was charged with designing and building a great system of decorative fountains in the royal gardens, work that took many years and showed rare talent. He built European houses in the garden enclosures and before one, Italian in style, set a curious water clock.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-non-expedit:
Non expedit, Latin for it is not expedient, was the Holy See's order keeping Italian Catholics from parliamentary polls after unification. Uncertainty followed Italy's 1861 constitution and anti-church laws of 1865 and 1866, until the Penitentiary's decree of 29 February 1868 fixed the motto neither elector nor elected.

Pius IX feared a deputy's oath would seem to bless the spoliation of the Holy See, and rigged elections made Catholic gains hopeless besides. The entry weighs that policy against the loss of Catholic voices like Cantù and Conti in parliament. Until 1868 a few eminent Catholics, including Cantù and Conti, still sat in parliament.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-paul-de-sorba:
Paul de Sorbait was a Viennese physician born in Hainault in 1624 and dead at Vienna on 19 April 1691. Schooled at Paderborn, he took philosophy and medicine doctorates at Padua, practised at Rome, Cologne, and Arnhem, and joined Vienna's medical faculty in August 1652. He became professor of theoretical medicine in 1655 and of practical medicine in 1666, and court physician to Empress-Dowager Eleonora in 1658.

In 1676 he rebuilt the Goldberg students' hall at his own cost and added a chapel. In the plague year 1679 Leopold I made him councillor and chief supervisor of Vienna's sanitation, and soon after ennobled him. He resigned his chair in 1681 and founded a medical scholarship. During the 1683 Turkish siege he commanded the student company as chief sergeant-major. His tomb lies in Saint Stephen's Cathedral, and Austrian doctors chose his portrait as their badge in 1909.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-peter-the-her:
Peter the Hermit was a preacher of the First Crusade whom legend wrongly made its author. Born at Amiens about 1050, he lived for years as a hermit before later chroniclers, Albert of Aix and William of Tyre, gave him the starring role. Their tales send him to Jerusalem, suffering at Turkish hands, dreaming of Christ in the Holy Sepulchre, and carrying the patriarch's letters to Urban II. Contemporary historians name him only among many crusade preachers.

The entry is firm: the crusade belongs to Urban II alone, and Peter preached only after Clermont. In March 1096 he led a people's band to Constantinople, lost it to massacre near Nicaea while seeking the emperor's help, and joined Godfrey's army in 1097. At Antioch he even tried to desert, though he later served as envoy to Kerbugha. Home again, he founded Neufmoutier monastery, dying there in 1115.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-philipp-veit:
Philipp Veit was a German Nazarene painter, born at Berlin in 1793 and grandson of the philosopher Mendelssohn. His mother Dorothea and her husband Friedrich Schlegel became Catholics in 1808, and he followed them into the Church in 1810, deciding about then to paint. After Dresden drawing lessons and a Vienna portrait attempt, he fought honourably in the War of Liberation in 1813, then went to Italy.

At Rome he studied under Overbeck and Cornelius as their best pupil. He painted the Temptation of Joseph and the Seven Years of Plenty for the Casa Zuccari frescoes, with colour fresher than his friends'. He replaced Cornelius on Dante's Paradise in the Villa Massimi and painted the lowest reaches of Dante's Heaven. Settling at Frankfurt in 1830 and Mainz in 1854, he crowned the Virgin at Trinità dei Monti and treated the Colosseum's reconsecration. He died at Mainz in 1877.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-st-deusd:
Deusdedit, also called Adeodatus I, was consecrated pope on 19 October 615, though one dating gives 13 November. He died on 8 November 618, though one dating gives 3 December. His birth date is unknown. He was distinguished for charity and zeal. He encouraged and supported clergy impoverished by political troubles.

When earthquake and leprosy struck his diocese, he set a heroic example in relief work. Only a few decretals bear his name, and none is authenticated. Report calls him the first pope to seal pontifical documents with lead, or bullae. One from his reign survives, showing the Good Shepherd among sheep with Alpha and Omega, and Deusdedit Papae on the reverse. His feast falls on 8 November.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pulpit:
A pulpit is an elevated stand to preach from, taking its name from the Latin pulpitum, a stage or scaffold. This encyclopedia entry finds its biblical forerunners in Solomon, who prayed from a brazen scaffold, and Esdras, who read the law from a wooden step. He also called the stand analogium, from the preaching of God's word, and ambo, from the way it wraps around the speaker.

The ambo was the direct ancestor of the modern pulpit. In the earliest Christian age the bishop preached from his chair, a memory kept in the French chaire and German Predigtstuhl. From the thirteenth century, rood-lofts called jubé rose in France, placed with reference to cross and altar. Pulpits of the modern kind appeared in Italy just as early. Niccola Pisano finished the Pisa pulpit in 1260, an unattached work on seven columns that opened a new path for Italian sculpture.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-saint-paul-th:
Paul the Hermit, also called Paul of Thebes, fled to the Egyptian desert as a youth of sixteen during the Decian persecution. He lived in a mountain cave until the age of one hundred and thirteen. His Life survives in three versions: Jerome's Latin text and two Greek forms, one much shorter. His entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia opens with the scholarly quarrel over which version came first.

Bidez, who published the Greek texts in 1900, held Jerome's Latin original, while Nau argued for the shorter Greek as the source. Setting that debate aside, the entry retells the shared story: Paul's flight, his long solitude, and Anthony's visit to the aged hermit, prompted by a vision that humbled Anthony's pride. It is a compact guide to a founding tale of desert monastic life.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-spirit:
Spirit, from Latin spiritus, to breathe, and Greek pneuma, names the principle of life pictured as a breath of air, and this entry sorts its several allied senses. Breath is the plainest sign of life and its stopping the sure mark of death, invisible and impalpable, standing for the unseen force behind vital processes.

The word covers a living, intelligent, bodiless being such as the soul, the fiery Stoic pneuma taken as a universal vital force. And refined bodily fluids once thought to mediate between mind and gross matter Animal spirits, vital spirits. And natural spirits were accepted agencies into the eighteenth century. And the entry shows how one word carried theology, philosophy, and old medicine at once.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-abban-the-: St. Abban the Hermit is known only in outline: an Irishman who lived at Abingdon in England, commemorated on 13 May, whose year of death is not certainly known. This brief entry places him before St. Patrick's time, making him a pre-Patrician figure of the early Irish Church in England.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-deusdedit:
Canterbury's sixth archbishop, Deusdedit, holds a quiet first: no Anglo-Saxon had held England's primacy before him. Born in Wessex under the Saxon name Frithona, Ithamar of Rochester consecrated him at Canterbury in 655 and held the see until his death on 14 July 664. This Catholic Encyclopedia entry of 1913 is frank about how little his nine years left behind.

Only one of his consecrations is certain, Damian of Rochester in 656, and claims about his part in founding Peterborough rest on a disputed charter. His death fell on the same day as Kent's King Erconbert, and Canterbury's St. Peter's porch received his burial. The entry's value lies in its restraint, marking the start of a long line of English archbishops with exactness rather than invention.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-vincenzo-de-v:
Vincenzo de Vit was an Italian Latinist who lived from 1810 to 1892. Born at Mestrina near Padua, he studied at Padua, was ordained in 1836, became librarian of Rovigo's Academy of Concordi and canon of its cathedral in 1844. Then, under Rosmini's influence, entered the Institute of Charity at Stresa, where he began revising Forcellini's Latin lexicon.

Needing libraries, he worked at Florence in 1861 and Rome from 1862, returning north each summer. Unlike Forcellini and Furlanetto, he aimed to cover every period and variety of Latin down to AD 568, digesting decadent authors and Church Fathers exactly and giving large space to inscriptions. His Lexicon of All Latinity, a third larger than Furlanetto's edition, was completed in 1879, though its bulk forced him to omit proper names. His Onomasticon reached only the letter P, and no one has finished it.
common-sense-how-to-exercise-it:
Common Sense, How to Exercise It presents the teachings of Yoritomo-Tashi, rendered from manuscripts his translator turned over leaf by leaf in a deserted room of a provincial museum. Common sense, the book argues, is nature's priceless gift and an income in itself. It solves problems of truth and conduct without bias from logic's subtleties or selfish interests.

The Shogun breaks the faculty into eight parts: perception, memory, thought, alertness, deduction, foresight, reason, and judgment. Each is discussed in turn, with its relations to the rest. Warnings follow against moral inertia, indifference, sentimentality, and egotism. The reward promised is a practical sense that sees things as they are and does things as they should be done.
cosmic-consciousness-the-man-god-whom-we:
A work on higher spiritual life, signed Ali Nomad and dated 1915, bears the title Cosmic Consciousness: The Man-God Whom We Await. Its first chapter calls the change it treats a new birth and gives cases said to show it. Faiths of East and West are set side by side from the start.

Later chapters draw on Buddha, Hindu saints, Japanese Zen training, and the maxims of Brother Lawrence. The writer argues that full awareness brings peace and bliss, not a loss of self. Tales of monks, temples, and holy men fill many pages. Readers meet a mix of lore, life stories, and teaching aimed at those who seek direct knowledge of the divine.
doe-osti-17019150-quantum-computing-for-:
Lawrence Livermore report LLNL-TR-2024431, dated September 2026, sums up project 24-ERD-054 on quantum computing for high energy density science. Yujin Cho, Zachary Espley, and Kristi Beck led the work, with Sandia and Los Alamos partners. The target is matter under extreme heat and pressure, where plain simulation trades accuracy against speed.

The team built methods to run small quantum simulations on a Livermore processor and to calibrate that hardware with automated feedback. They calibrated six qubits at once, a job that can take hours by hand, and ran a two qubit simulation using dynamical mean field theory. Gate tests showed a circuit with one two qubit gate matched the ideal result most closely.
doe-osti-17046757-grazing-angle-estimate:
Technical note by Boris Podobedov of Brookhaven National Laboratory, dated September 2026, estimates a worst case beam accident angle for the future Electron-Ion Collider. In the Hadron Storage Ring, a stored 275 GeV proton beam could, under a fast instability driven by a crab cavity, swing sideways and graze the beam pipe wall. The note defines that maximum credible incident for safety studies.

Deliberately harsh assumptions are used: machine protection fails to stop the beam, collimators stay out, and the instability grows unchecked. A simplified beam motion model with ring lattice data then bounds the grazing angle. Results stay below about 5 milliradians in the regular arcs and below 9 milliradians outside a zone near the interaction point.
doe-osti-17197467-extending-the-supervis:
Jihoon Chung, Jamie Lian, and Borui Cui of Oak Ridge ask whether a building control kit built for small offices can move into small factories, in report ORNL/TM-2026/4735 dated September 2026. The kit is a supervisory controller package made for small and medium commercial buildings. Industrial sites differ in loads, schedules, and gear, so the transfer needs checking first.

The assessment is literature based. The team gathered published work and sorted it by topic, then focused on six target manufacturing industries. For each, they weighed what the kit does today against plant needs: process loads, ventilation demands, and control points. Findings judge where the kit fits as is, where it needs changes, and where it does not fit at all.
doe-osti-17198163-design-of-defensive-cy:
Lee Maccarone, Robert Lois, and Robert Brulles of Sandia set out how to design defensive cybersecurity for microreactors, in report SAND2026-27276R dated September 2026. Microreactors are small, often remote power units with digital controls. Their defenses must be designed in from the start, not bolted on after the plant is built.

The method rests on a tiered cybersecurity analysis with three levels of depth, each with its own semantic model. Design work is aligned with the phases of plant design, so protections mature alongside the hardware. Chapters define defensive architecture elements and strategies, then treat decoupling: ways to keep vital control paths apart from attack paths. An appendix lists the fundamental sensors and actuators a microreactor presents to its defenders.
doe-osti-2588039-hazardous-waste-facilit:
Luciana Vigil-Holterman wrote the 2025 update of Los Alamos National Laboratory's Hazardous Waste Facility Permit Community Relations Plan, LA-UR-25-28726, issued August 27, 2025. The plan is a regulatory document: it commits the laboratory to a defined way of keeping the public informed and consulted about its hazardous waste facility permit. It exists because the permit requires it, and it is refreshed on a fixed cycle.

The plan explains who is consulted, how information flows out, and how comments flow back in. A fillable form lets residents give feedback on the plan itself, and the laboratory uses that dialog to inform its decisions. Each year the laboratory requests specific feedback for the next update, which is published by September 1. Comments and suggestions received are compiled and posted. For nearby communities, this is the standing map of how to be heard on waste operations at the site.
doe-osti-2588182-applying-linear-optics-:
Xi Yang of Brookhaven National Laboratory wrote this technical note, BNL-228832-2025-TECH, in August 2025. Xiaobiao Huang and Victor Smaluk share credit for the work. It presents a fast way to align the harmonic sextupole magnets of NSLS-II, the laboratory's 3 GeV synchrotron light source, where tiny magnet misalignments spoil beam quality.

The method, called LOCOM, modulates the closed orbit with sine-wave signals at two fast correctors, phased to span the betatron phase space. Simulations show that combining it with half-millimeter local orbit bumps resolves sextupole field offsets to better than 10 percent of the sextupole strength. That translates to alignment finer than 50 micrometers. Machine-learning-optimized bumps keep the orbit stable even when sextupole strengths swing by plus or minus 40 percent. Short measurement times of a few minutes limit drift and hysteresis errors, and proof-of-principle measurements at NSLS-II validate the approach.
doe-osti-2588300-mesa-packaging-and-inte: Spalding Craft, Daniel Garcia, and Lawrence Klebesadel of Sandia National Laboratories prepared this single capability slide, SAND2025-10996R, dated April 25, 2025. It inventories the packaging and integration services of MESA, Sandia's microsystems complex. The listed capabilities cover flip chip and wire bonding. They also cover wafer-to-wafer and die-to-wafer direct bond interconnect. Plating for through-silicon vias, sputter and evaporation metallization, and lithography up to eight-inch wafers appear as well. Precision die thinning and solder jetting round out the list, aimed at national security programs.
doe-osti-2589587-viscosity-measurements-:
Sandia National Laboratories report SAND2025-11791R, by Joshua Townsend, Jeremiah Boerner, Thomas Gardiner, and co-authors, measures and models how materials flow under extreme shock. Viscosity, a fluid's resistance to flow, is hard to measure at the pressures reached in fusion experiments and high-speed impacts. Wrong values distort the computer models used to design those experiments.

Atom-level simulations using density functional theory supplied viscosity estimates through the Green-Kubo method, which reads stress fluctuations over time. Worked examples follow fused silica along its main shock curve and beryllium behavior under conditions tied to the MagLIF fusion platform. Hydrodynamic codes then used the new values to model viscous shocks. Mesh studies show the region near a corrugated boundary drives cost, with runs near 350,000 elements. The values sharpen predictions for Sandia's pulsed-power work.
doe-osti-2998230-one-dimensional-multi-v:
Los Alamos National Laboratory report LA-UR-25-30084, issued 10 October 2025, upgrades how the FLAG hydrodynamics code handles materials in contact. Conrad Delgado, Spiros Manolas, Nathanial Vaughn-Kukura, and Mikhail Shashkov wrote it. FLAG models violent events where materials collide, slide, and separate. Older contact logic could not track each material's own velocity where materials share a cell, which blocks coupling to other physics.

The new one-dimensional algorithm advances each material on its own mesh. It then applies a contact force computed from how much the materials overfill each other. That force pulls positions back into line with a single shared mesh. An optional remap can then add or remove void in a cell. Test cases in one dimension converge to known analytical answers where they exist. The work is a stepping stone toward the same freedom in two and three dimensions.
doe-osti-3001096-detector-response-and-b:
Gabriel Lopez, a summer intern in Sandia's organisation 9228, reports in SAND2025-13701R, dated August 2025, on whether battery power quietly degrades nuclear material measurements. Sandia's Material Control and Accountability team confirms special nuclear material with high-purity germanium detectors, which identify isotopes by their gamma-ray fingerprints. Two portable units, an AEGIS and an ORTEC model, can run purely on battery, yet their behaviour on battery was undocumented.

Lopez tested the AEGIS across battery charge ranges, wall charging and hot swaps, changing batteries mid-measurement without stopping. The working assumptions were that battery changes would fail some quality control checks, and that charge times would matter most. Measurements were scored pass or fail against the team's quality control tests, hunting trends. The intern report records the setup, data and patterns, giving the accountability team evidence for how far field measurements can trust a battery.
doe-osti-3002086-fy-2025-end-of-year-rep:
Monica Maceira, Omar Marcillo, and Erin Cunningham close out a year of seismic work in Oak Ridge report ORNL/SPR-2025/4220, dated September 2025. The National Nuclear Security Administration's safeguards office funded the project. It watches for underground vibration sources, such as blasts, using two kinds of sensors. One is the standard seismometer and geophone. The other is distributed acoustic sensing, which turns a fiber-optic cable into a line of vibration sensors.

The team built a database of continuous recordings plus known events for checking results. They tested ways to spot unusual events and to locate them from geophone and fiber data. Fiber-based locations from signal strength look promising, but scaling is hard without enough standard seismometers nearby. Moving events also break the strength-based method, the authors caution.
doe-osti-3005945-tex-chlorine-highly-enr:
Final benchmark documentation for TEX-Chlorine (IER-499) fills 211 pages on a set of critical experiments run on the Comet assembly machine at the National Criticality Experiments Research Center in Nevada. Eric Aboud and Jesse Norris of Lawrence Livermore are the evaluators, with Paul Maggi as internal reviewer. The work varies the Thermal/Epithermal eXperiments (TEX) baseline by adding sodium chloride absorber plates to highly enriched uranium plates, with high-density polyethylene as moderator and reflector. Three configurations were run between July and August 2024, the first two thermal in spectrum and the third fast.

Each case gives a benchmark keff drawn from the measured reactor period, with an uncertainty budget built from 33 components and corrections for model simplifications. The ICSBEP technical review group accepted all three cases in April 2025, and the evaluation went to ICSBEP in August 2025. An appendix prints full MCNP 6.3.0 input listings using ENDF/B-VIII.0 data.
doe-osti-3005964-ier-620-pulsed-neutron-:
Lawrence Livermore's P. Maggi signs this August 2025 memo closing the CED-3a phase of IER-620, a pulsed-neutron die-away campaign on oil targets. The PNDA testbed checks thermal scattering laws against measured neutron decay. Earlier campaigns covered plastic and water targets (IER-501 and IER-580). This one adds three hydrogen-rich liquids tied to machining work with fissionable material: Mobilmet 423 cutting oil, Mobil Teresstic 220 lubricating oil, and propylene glycol, a common coolant ingredient.

The neutron generator, detectors, shielding box, and aluminum sample containers carry over unchanged from the earlier work. Container volumes run from 78 milliliters to 25 liters. Because the two oils are made to performance specs rather than fixed chemistry, their makeup can vary, and the memo flags handling needs found during work planning. Product and safety data sheets for all three liquids are appended, and added materials are budgeted below $5,000.
doe-osti-3010353-final-report-ufl-rapids:
Final report for the RAPIDS2 SciDAC Institute, DOE grant DE-SC0021320, by Sanjay Ranka of the University of Florida, covers learned compression of scientific data for high-performance computing. The institute's charge was to make machine learning reduction safe for simulation science.

The framework developed across its papers pairs autoencoder and generative models with explicit error bounds and per-instance constraints. Nonlinear-by-linear decompositions keep provable distortion limits while the learned parts do the heavy shrinking. Constraint satisfaction protects derived quantities of interest, the numbers scientists actually publish, after compression. The work is presented as the bridge between modern generative models and the strict reliability demands of simulation workflows.
doe-osti-3017114-ier-620-pulsed-neutron-:
Paul Maggi of Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory wrote this August 2025 report on IER-620, a pulsed-neutron die-away experiment with oil targets. It records completion of the CED-3a phase, the experiment initiation step in the lab's criticality safety process. The testbed measures how neutron pulses die away in hydrogen-rich materials, which validates the thermal scattering data used in safety calculations.

Earlier campaigns ran the same testbed on plastic and Lucite targets, and on water. This campaign adds three hydrogenous oils tied to machining work with fissionable materials. The neutron generator, detectors, shielding box, and aluminum sample containers carry over unchanged. Phase 3a work identified and started buying the needed materials, and began work control changes. Safety analysts get the groundwork for benchmarks on materials that surround real machining operations.
doe-osti-3017860-understanding-and-contr:
David T Limmer of the University of California, Berkeley, wrote this final technical report for Early Career award DE-SC0020121. The project studied molecules in complex environments after light strikes them: what happens after light energizes a molecule inside a liquid or material, where the surroundings jostle every step. Predicting photochemical outcomes is hard because fluctuations make results statistical, and events run faster than equilibrium thinking allows.

The team built accurate, fast simulation tools for irreversible processes across scales. They applied them to electron transfer under exotic conditions, where spin and topology opened new reaction pathways. Light harvesting systems, where energy and charge transport couple, were another target. One line of work traced the origins of fast triplet formation in a metal-free system, tying solvent motion and electronic polarizability to recombination rates. The stated products are design principles for nanoscale energy materials and molecular machines.
doe-osti-3020953-design-of-defensive-cyb:
Sandia National Laboratories report SAND2025-12466R, by Lee T. Maccarone, Robert J. Brulles, Michael T. Rowland, and Jenna deCastro, designs defensive cybersecurity architecture for sodium-cooled fast reactors. Such an architecture arranges a plant's digital systems so that the functions most significant to safety, security, and safeguards get the strongest protection. An attacker should have to defeat multiple, diverse, independent measures before reaching anything that matters.

The team mapped the instrumentation and control architecture of sodium-cooled fast reactors, including the Natrium design's reactor protection and engineered safety features, and traced how systems depend on each other. The analysis follows the Tiered Cybersecurity Analysis approach in the NRC's draft guide DG-5075 for plants licensed under 10 CFR Part 53. From the dependency map, the authors derive the passive requirements the architecture must impose throughout the plant's life.
doe-osti-3023850-improbability-of-post-c:
Rob P Rechard, Benjamin Reedlunn, James E Bean Jr, Brad A Day, and Lawrence C Sanchez of Sandia National Laboratories. They assess a deep-time safety question for the Waste Isolation Pilot Plant in SAND2026-18392, printed March 2026. Transuranic waste containers buried in salt will slowly be squeezed as the salt creeps shut. Could compacting an array of containers ever stack fissile material into a critical configuration?

The analysis models arrays of pipe overpack containers packed in a hexagonal layout. Even a large trapezoidal block fall onto a filled room left the containers with negligible deformation and disruption in the simulations. The title states the verdict plainly: post-closure criticality in the compacted array is improbable. Supporting sections work through the scenarios and material assumptions behind that screening call.
doe-osti-3023852-improbability-of-post-c:
Sandia National Laboratories report SAND2026-18395, printed March 2026, screens the same deep-time question for a different package: criticality control overpacks buried at the Waste Isolation Pilot Plant. Rob P Rechard, Brad A Day, Benjamin Reedlunn, and James E Bean Jr wrote it. These overpacks are built to keep fissile waste safely subcritical, and the question is whether room closure and compaction could ever defeat that control.

The evaluation caps waste mass at 54.5 kilograms per overpack, then adds margin: where the authorized beryllium and beryllium oxide content is 0.545 kilograms, the study models 0.585 kilograms, a 7 percent increase. It also revisits earlier pipe overpack work across three water regimes and checks how hydrogen-bearing filler materials change the allowable masses. The screening conclusion matches the title: criticality is improbable.
doe-osti-3031028-transformational-molecu:
Miao Yu of the University at Buffalo, Patrick T. Underhill of Rensselaer Polytechnic Institute, Shiguang Li of GTI Energy, and partners report under award DE-FE0031730 on tailor-made sorbents for post-combustion carbon capture. The period ran from October 2019, with the report issued in April 2026. Their method, molecular layer deposition, coats a support one molecular layer at a time to build pores that sieve carbon dioxide by size from power plant exhaust.

Process simulations tested a vacuum swing system built on a titanium-bearing zeolite, Ti-13X. One grid of runs used 8 units with 3 feed beds and 6 light reflux beds, at 40 degrees Celsius and low vacuum of 20 to 25 kilopascals. Outputs tracked carbon dioxide purity and recovery in the heavy product, plus stray oxygen content in parts per million.
doe-osti-3365151-technical-note-sabrs-3-:
Los Alamos National Laboratory technical note LA-UR-26-24172, by Brian Larsen and dated April 28, 2026, hunts for hidden rhythms in data from the SABRS-3 ZEP D3 space detector. The search ran from February 2022 through April 2026, prompted by a sister instrument, NRL's SIRI-2, reporting a 5-minute periodicity in 2026. A repeating signal could betray instrument trouble or real space weather structure.

The 5-minute signal is not there: the band stays below detection thresholds in every year, including 2026. An apparent 18.6-hour peak in 2023 data weakened under Lomb-Scargle analysis, which found many comparable peaks between 12 and 30 hours, and different years favor different periods, arguing against a stable physical signal. Correlations with the geomagnetic Kp index were weak, explaining under 6 percent of variance even at the best 48-hour lag.
doe-osti-3366081-triboelectric-nanogener:
Los Alamos National Laboratory issued report LA-UR-26-24429, by William Mikhel James and Collin Thomas Rise, issued May 27, 2026, asks an unfashionable question about triboelectric nanogenerators: can anyone reproduce the numbers? These devices harvest energy from rubbing films, and the literature chases record outputs while rarely checking whether results repeat. The study tests repeatability and reproducibility head-on.

Five polymers, Kapton, polyethylene, PET, PTFE, and PVDF, were paired in all 25 combinations for reproducibility runs, with three pairs chosen for repeatability. A shaker table swept excitation from near zero to 5 kilohertz over 30-second cycles while films contacted and separated. Gold conductive layers faced outward in each device. The verdict on consistency, whatever it is, matters more for the field's credibility than another record output.
doe-osti-3367030-tribological-behavior-o:
Oak Ridge National Laboratory report ORNL/TM-2026/4617, by Tomas Grejtak, Nidia Gallego, and Jun Qu, documents sliding friction and wear tests on nuclear graphite in hot inert gas. Graphite components rub in pebble-bed and fluoride-salt reactors, and their wear rates feed design life calculations. The June 2026 report completes an Advanced Reactor Technologies milestone on initial wear and abrasion studies.

ET-10 graphite pins and flats slid against each other across loads, speeds, and temperatures up to 650 degrees Celsius. At the higher load, friction coefficients ran 0.59 to 0.65 initially and settled lower, with wear rates in the range of 3.2 to 4.9 times ten to the minus five. Sliding polished both surfaces smoother and brighter. Load mattered more than speed or temperature for the flat's wear, while pin and flat wore by visibly different patterns.
doe-osti-3377992-industrial-conduit-hydr:
Industrial Conduit Hydropower Opportunities in the United States: Scoping Assessment, Oak Ridge National Laboratory report ORNL/TM-2025/4269, comes from the Environmental Sciences Division. Four authors are printed: Scott DeNeale, Lindsay Ashworth, Antonia Chu, and Evelyn Kalmar. Conduit hydropower puts turbines inside existing pipes and canals that already move water for industry, farms, or cities, so no new dam is built.

As a scoping assessment, the report sizes the national opportunity before judging individual sites. It works from the stock of industrial conduits in the country and asks how much power their flows could reasonably generate. The cover is dated July 2026 while the internal title page reads March 2026; either way the study is a first-pass map of where conduit projects deserve a closer look.
doe-osti-3382300-fluorinated-glyme-solve:
Navitas Advanced Solutions Group delivers the final technical report for award DE-EE0009645, dated July 20, 2026. The subject is fluorinated glyme solvents to extend lithium-sulfur battery life. Thomas Vaid is named principal investigator and Amy DeCormier technical lead. Argonne National Laboratory was the subrecipient. The project ran from October 1, 2021 to September 30, 2025 under a Vehicle Technologies Office funding call.

The milestones track the solvent, called PFG, from bench to scale. Targets included electrolyte conductivity of at least 10 millisiemens per centimeter. They also included a cathode delivering over 1100 milliamp-hours per gram in the new electrolyte. The team verified a protection layer forming on both anode and cathode. It cut polysulfide dissolution by more than 70 percent against the baseline. It also scaled PFG synthesis up to 200 grams per batch.
doe-osti-3403179-layer-time-control-for-:
Oak Ridge report ORNL/TM-2026/4678 tackles layer timing in large scale additive manufacturing, meaning very large 3D printing. Seokpum Kim leads a team from Oak Ridge, the University of Tennessee, Haddy Inc., and Arizona State University. The work sits under CRADA number NFE-24-10074.

Print layers must cool enough, but not too much, before the next layer lands. The team used high performance computing and heat models to set that timing. One case starts layers at 130 seconds with material laid at 220 degrees Celsius. A 61-layer data set then guides timing across part angles and spots.
doe-osti-3520826-fy2025-light-water-reac:
Oak Ridge plan ORNL/SPR-2025/4223, dated September 2025, sets the Fiscal 2025 materials research path for the Light Water Reactor Sustainability Program. Xiang Chen, Yann Le Pape, and Leonard S. Fifield wrote the plan. Keeping current reactors running safely for more years is the program's aim.

Topics span oxide strengthening, new alloys, and behavior under irradiation. Such work guides material choices for next-generation reactors too. The plan ties material innovation to regulatory acceptance steps. Utility owners get a research map for life extension claims. Each topic names the evidence regulators will expect before approving longer operation.
doe-osti-3547195-fusel-alcohol-fermentat:
Sandia report SAND2026-25444R, by Claire Louise Bartlett and dated August 20, 2026, ferments fusel alcohols and recovers them in place with extractive overlays. Fusel alcohols can feed sustainable aviation fuel routes. Aviation needs dense liquid fuels, so bio routes matter.

Yeast cells grew on agar plates, then in small broth tubes overnight. Cultures grew at 37 degrees Celsius and 250 rotations per minute. One insert held 160 microliters of pure ethyl acetate as overlay. Overlays pull product out as cells make it, easing toxicity. Students and fuel researchers get a compact bench method to test.
doe-osti-3682478-next-generation-wall-re:
Oak Ridge report ORNL/SPR-2026/4725, dated June 2026, gives the first post-retrofit year for wall panels with built-in vacuum insulation. Emishaw Iffa and Andre Desjarlais are the two printed authors. The panels went onto two occupied apartment buildings in Albany, New York, between September 2024 and January 2025. Vacuum panels insulate strongly in a thin layer, but they also block vapour. That raised worry about trapped moisture inside the walls.

Sensors were commissioned in March 2025, copying the layout of a twenty-two-month baseline study. Paired sensors in each wall layer logged heat, damp, and heat flow every hour. Readings cover April 1, 2025 through March 31, 2026. Moisture in the board layers rose in summer and fell in winter, as expected. All layers stayed well below the moisture level that risks board decay. Computer models of heat and moisture flow round out the field data.
essay-upon-wit:
Sir Richard Blackmore defends a low place for laughter in his Essay upon Wit of 1716, reprinted by the Augustan Reprint Society in May 1946 with Joseph Addison's Freeholder paper No. 45 of the same year and an introduction by Richard C. Boys. Blackmore opens with man's degenerate pull toward pleasures of sense. Next to those, he grants, the light and facetious quality that produces mirth is admired in all ages.

His verdict is stern: wit unbends the mind and refreshes the spirits for study, but it is the meanest province of the intellect, the least beneficial. Addison's commentary stands alongside as the cooler voice. The reprint opens a series on wit for scholars of the Augustan age.
five-children-and-it:
E. Nesbit sent five children digging in a Kent gravel pit, where they woke the Psammead, a grumpy sand-fairy who grants one wish a day. The children are Cyril, Anthea, Robert, and Jane, with a baby brother called the Lamb. Each wish lasts only until sunset, and each goes wrong in a fresh way.

They wish to be beautiful, to find gold guineas, to have wings, and to be grown up, and undo the damage by teatime. Nesbit tells the mishaps in a dry, funny voice that treats magic as a household nuisance. Five Children and It became a model for later children's fantasy: ordinary children, real tempers, and wishes that teach care in asking.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-LeibowitzJeffMa: nsia-LeibowitzJeffMaterials1-74 Leibowitz Jeff Materials 1-74: the made public government document, captured as titled. Subject: government records. A bare file, kept as issued. An obscure item, filed. From the archive shelves, for readers of the files and readers.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-PoliticalMorali:
Hundreds of citizens signed this pledge during the Vietnam era. They refused to pay their federal income taxes voluntarily while American forces were used, in their words, in violation of the Constitution, international law, and the United Nations Charter. The pledge names Vietnam and the invasion of the Dominican Republic. It also charges American indifference to crimes committed in the signers' names.

War tax refusal was a disciplined form of protest: sign, refuse, and accept the penalties. A printed pledge with hundreds of names turned private conscience into public record. The document preserves the movement's legal argument in its own words. It also preserves its moral one, that paying for a war is a choice for which each taxpayer answers.
griboyedov-verstand-schafft-leiden-woe-f:
Chatsky returns to Moscow full of wit and ideals and finds society stupid, corrupt, and ready to call him mad. Alexander Griboyedov's verse comedy Woe from Wit appears here in German translation as Verstand schafft Leiden. Written in 1824, the play became the masterpiece of Russian drama before Chekhov.

Nearly every line of Griboyedov's verse passed into proverb; Russians quote it the way English speakers quote Shakespeare. Famusov's stuffy household, the silent Molchalin, and Chatsky's blazing monologues fill a single ballroom with a whole society. The comedy circulated in manuscript for years because censors feared it. German readers receive a classic whose home audience knows it by heart. Few national literatures rest so much on one play.
hasisadra-s-adventure-essay-7-from-scien:
Thomas Henry Huxley retold the Babylonian flood story in Hasisadra's Adventure, the seventh essay of Science and Hebrew Tradition. Huxley begins with the tale itself: Hasisadra of Surippak dreams of a coming deluge, builds a ship caulked with bitumen, and rides out six days of storm. He sends out a dove, a swallow, and a raven, exactly as Noah would, then sacrifices on a mountain.

The story survives, Huxley explains, on a clay tablet from Assurbanipal's library at Nineveh, copied from a far older original known before 2000 B.C. His point lands quietly: the Hebrew flood narrative has a Babylonian elder brother, and geology and criticism, not mockery, must settle what that means. It is Huxley's science-versus-scripture campaign in miniature.
highroads-of-geography-introductory-book:
This school geography reader came out in 1916, in the Royal School Series. A father leaves home for a year of travel round the world. His children learn geography from the letters he sends back. Each stop on the route becomes a short, plain lesson for young readers.

Letters come from France, Egypt, India, Burma, and Ceylon. Later stops add China, Japan, and Canada, with notes on native peoples and Eskimos. The chapters mix story with facts on streets, dress, food, and work. At the end father comes home, and review exercises close the book.
hindu-tales-from-the-sanskrit:
S M Mitra translated these Hindu tales from the Sanskrit. Mrs Arthur Bell adapted them for English readers, in an edition of 1919. The note says some tales come from India's ancient classics. Others passed by word of mouth for hundreds of years before print.

Nine tales tell of magic pitchers, clever thieves, and hermits' daughters. A magic shoe, a jewelled arrow, and a silken thread all play their parts. The note praises the tales as tools for shaping the young. Children and adults alike get short, bright stories with a moral grain of self-knowledge.
how-to-do-it:
Edward Everett Hale wrote these papers of counsel for young people. Hale follows a large set of named youths through success and failure. Alice, Bob, Clara, and Horace recur as his living examples. The chapters sort life into skills: how to talk, write, read, and travel.

School life, vacations, and life alone each get a turn. Church habits and life with children and elders follow. Hale urges Stephen to get great men's lives into his blood and brain. Sixteen world leaders' books are his tonic in one letter. The tone is fatherly, brisk, and moral. It is a famed Victorian guide to doing life well.
humoresque-a-laugh-on-life-with-a-tear-b:
Fannie Hurst published these stories in 1920, under a subtitle that promises a laugh with a tear behind it. The title story opens on the Bowery and Mulberry Street. Seventeen languages steam from the tenements, Hurst writes. A frontispiece shows a boy capering through a Dvořák melody.

Oats for the Woman, White Goods, and The Wrong Pew follow. Roody, in one tale, haggles over a sewing machine ten dollars cheaper than last week. People must be amused as they must be fed, he argues. Hurst writes the Jewish and immigrant quarters with heat and sentiment. Music, hunger, and ambition drive her small dreamers.
indiscreet-letters-from-peking-being-the:
B. L. Putnam Weale edited Indiscreet Letters From Peking, notes of an eye-witness to the siege of 1900. The China edition here is dated 1922, from Shanghai. Parts cover the warning, the siege, and the sack. Boxers approach, barricades rise, and an ultimatum comes in the first part.

Starving children strip trees of leaves in Prince Su's grounds during the siege. Mothers drink huge amounts of water to stave off hunger, the notes say. Shells, sorties, hospitals, and graveyards fill the daily record. Weale presents the legations' ordeal as raw diary, not polished history.
lectures-on-evolution-essay-3-from-scien:
Thomas Henry Huxley's Lectures on Evolution form the third essay in Science and Hebrew Tradition. Huxley opens with the vast diversity of Nature itself. Just ideas about that system, he says, matter deeply to everyone.

Humans are tiny points in extent and brief in duration, he admits. Still, our past history can be studied with care. He sets out three hypotheses about the history of nature. Evidence, not scripture or guesswork, must judge between them. The essay shows Huxley teaching evolution to a broad public. The lectures were first given to American audiences. Huxley's tour made evolution a headline topic across the Atlantic.
lectures-on-the-english-poets-delivered-:
William Hazlitt delivered his Lectures on the English Poets at the Surrey Institution. The second edition appeared in 1819, and this text was proofed against it. An introductory lecture on poetry in general opens the course.

Hazlitt moves through England's great poets with bold judgments. His lectures helped define the Romantic view of poetry. Feeling, power, and imagination matter more to him than rules. Audiences heard criticism performed like literature itself. These talks remain among the finest short guides to English verse. Chaucer, Shakespeare, and Milton anchor his course. Hazlitt's own prose burns with the gusto he praises.
life-and-habit:
Samuel Butler first published this book in 1878, then revised it. A 1910 edition added a preface by R. A. Streatfeild. Butler inscribed the work to Charles Paine Pauli, his barrister friend. Pauli had criticized the proof sheets of this and earlier books.

Streatfeild notes thirty-three years of change since the book first appeared. Many mighty figures had fallen, and humble ones risen, meanwhile. Butler's title joins two subjects: how life works and how habit shapes it. The book remains a key statement of his thinking about living things. The 1910 reprint followed in 1924 from Butler and Tanner. Butler dedicated his gratitude for Pauli's criticism across many books.
little-dorrit:
Charles Dickens sets this novel around the Marshalsea debtors' prison. His preface to the 1857 edition heads the contents. Book the First, called Poverty, lists thirty-six chapters. Sun and Shadow opens the story in Marseilles heat.

Amy Dorrit appears as the Child of the Marshalsea early. Her father earns the title Father of the Marshalsea. Chapters promise the whole science of government in satire. Fortune-telling, conspirators, and Mrs. Flintwinch's dreams thicken the plot. Bleeding Heart Yard and the lock introduce Marshalsea society. Little Dorrit's party and Mrs. Flintwinch's second dream follow.
martin-chuzzlewit:
Charles Dickens wrote Martin Chuzzlewit, a novel named for its young hero. His preface names greed and selfish pride as the book's core faults. He points to Mr. Pecksniff and to Jonas Chuzzlewit as key cases.

Dickens says Jonas grew cruel from the way he was raised and praised. Vice learned at home, he argues, falls back on the old man at last. The preface also defends the American part of the tale from claims of mere mockery. He also notes how crime in one home can breed crime in the next. The tale's humor sits close to that stern moral thread.
mary-jane-her-visit:
Mary Jane: Her Visit, by Clara Ingram Judson, came out in 1918. Barse and Hopkins printed it in New York and Newark. Frances White drew the pictures, as she did for Her Book.

Mary Jane rides the train to Glenville and explores a farm. She hunts for eggs, gardens with Grandfather, and learns to cook. Odd bundles, a garden thief, and a strawberry social add fun. A picnic at Flatrock comes just before she goes home again. Cousin John's visit and Grandfather's treat break up the farm days. The visit ends with the trip home, rested and full of tales.
meyer-us4798661-gas-generator-voltage-co:
Stanley A Meyer received United States Patent 4,798,661 on January 17, 1989, for a gas generator voltage control circuit. The circuit watches over the cell in his water fuel cell system. It is one of the later filings in his eight-patent family.

The design senses how much gas the cell is making and adjusts the voltage to match. Meyer wanted steady gas flow without wasting power or overheating the cell. The drawings show the sensors, the control loop, and the safety cutoffs. A patent proves a design was new on paper only. An Ohio court found Meyer's claims fraudulent in 1996.
michelangelo-a-collection-of-fifteen-pic:
Estelle M. Hurll edited this volume in the Riverside Art Series, published at Boston in 1900. It gathers fifteen pictures by Michelangelo, plus a portrait of the master. Hurll supplies an introduction and an interpretation for each work. A frontispiece portrait, attributed to Bugiardini, comes from the Uffizi Gallery in Florence.

The pictures include the Madonna and Child, the David, the Moses, and the Pietà. Hurll adds a directory of the works, collateral readings, and a table of the artist's life. She also lists his famous Italian contemporaries. The series aimed to put guided art study into the hands of ordinary readers.
mohammedanism-lectures-on-its-origin-its:
C. Snouck Hurgronje delivered these lectures in the American Lectures on the History of Religions series of 1914 and 1915. The printed volume followed in 1916. Hurgronje was professor of Arabic at the University of Leiden in Holland. His subject is Islam's origin, its religious and political growth, and its present state.

The lecture committee, founded in 1892, brought leading European scholars to American cities. Courses ran in Baltimore, Boston, Chicago, New York, and Philadelphia, among others. Hurgronje had studied Islam in Mecca and advised the Dutch colonial government. His lectures gave American audiences a scholar's survey of a faith then little understood in the West.
mrs-peter-rabbit:
Thornton W. Burgess published this animal tale in 1919, with pictures by Harrison Cady. Peter Rabbit has lost his appetite and feels lonesome. The contents send him on a trip to the Old Pasture. Hooty the Owl and sharp claws threaten the way.

Peter finds strange tracks and meets Little Miss Fuzzytail. Old Jed Thumper gets fooled along the way. Burgess wrote these bedtime tales to teach nature with charm. Each short chapter ends with a hook for the next. The book tells how Peter found a mate, told as soft adventure for young children.
nasa-tm-19630004521-the-explorer-xvi-mic:
Earl C. Hastings, Jr. compiled this NASA memorandum, TM X-824, in April 1963. It gives early results from the Explorer XVI satellite. That craft was built to count hits from micrometeoroids, tiny space grains. This supplement covers January 14 to March 2, 1963.

Hastings reports that thin pressure cells on the craft were punctured. Twenty-four cells of the thinner type had been holed by March 2. Six cells of the thicker type had been holed as well. Rates per square foot per day are given for both kinds. The counts were then matched against rates predicted before launch. Such data told engineers how much shielding real satellites would need.
nasa-tm-19650011719-space-operations-con: Volume 5, number 3 of the Space Operations Control Center satellite situation report is preserved here only as garbled scan text, with no readable body pages. No list of satellites, dates, or figures can be recovered from the hosted sample at all. The title and catalog note alone identify it as a NASA report on orbiting satellites and their current situation in orbit.
nasa-tm-19660002338-nuclear-rocket-simul: Nuclear rocket simulator tests, beginning with a run on flow initiation at thirty-five pounds per square inch with no turbine gas tank pressure, are named in the title of this NASA report. The catalog note adds that a liquid hydrogen run checked operating steps for instruments and data systems. The hosted sample preserves no readable body text, so no author, center, date, or test results can be grounded from it.
nasa-tm-19660009070-a-review-of-fatigue-:
Herbert F Hardrath at Langley reviewed fatigue research across the United States for an international meeting in Munich in June 1965. His scope is work done in government laboratories or under government support. Fatigue is the slow cracking of parts under repeated load. It remains a leading cause of structural failure in aircraft.

Topics in the review, per the catalog note, run from acoustic fatigue to crack growth and detection. Supersonic transport materials and structural fatigue both appear. A national review lets each laboratory see what the others have learned. Hardrath's survey served that purpose at a meeting of the International Committee on Aeronautical Fatigue, where countries compared notes.
nasa-tm-19660022058-effect-of-orientatio:
Ralph G Garlick at Lewis Research Center studied how tungsten crystals turn from ductile to brittle, and how that change depends on the crystal's direction. Tungsten is a very hard, heat-proof metal. Below a certain temperature it snaps instead of bending. Garlick tested single crystals of zone-refined tungsten, pulled along three named directions, in his summary.

Transition behavior proved highly dependent on orientation, he reports. One direction gave a sharp change and the lowest transition point in his tests. Reduction in area of the pulled specimens served as his measure. Direction matters because a crystal's inner planes are not the same each way. Such data guide the use of tungsten in hot, stressed parts.
nasa-tm-19670002001-space-power-system-m:
L. Rosenblum, C. M. Scheuermann, and T. A. Moss, of NASA's Lewis Research Center in Cleveland, prepared this paper for an alkali metal coolants symposium held in Vienna, Austria, in late 1966. It reports tests of whether niobium and tantalum tubing alloys could survive boiling potassium inside a turboelectric space power system.

Eight alloys were screened in sealed reflux capsule tests at very high temperatures, some for up to 10,000 hours. A second test ran a flowing two-phase loop that copied real power system flow and temperature conditions. Alloys containing reactive elements such as zirconium or hafnium resisted corrosion well. Alloys without those elements all showed significant corrosion. The authors link the resistance to those elements binding oxygen into a stable oxide.
nasa-tm-19680001382-the-structure-of-the:
Isadore Harris, of the Goddard Space Flight Center, and Wolfgang Priester, of the University of Bonn in Germany, examine the thermosphere's daily rhythm. The thermosphere is the high, thin layer where satellites drag. Its structure and variations are the paper's twin subjects.

The daily variation, they argue, is the key to understanding the whole layer. It governs the energy balance: heating, heat loss, conduction, and convection. Earlier calculations, from 1962, failed to place the daily density peak at its observed mid-afternoon time. Those attempts left out sideways interaction. Newer wind calculations, driven by pressure differences, are then considered.
nasa-tm-19680026115-resonant-perturbatio:
C. A. Wagner of Goddard Space Flight Center studies resonant perturbations of Earth satellites in this September 1968 report. Some orbits repeat their ground tracks in step with Earth's rotation. Those commensurable orbits feel strong pulls from longitude terms in Earth's gravity field.

Until recently, only roughly one-day resonant orbits were known. Wagner reports resonant effects on orbits repeating only in about two days. A June 1968 survey found two such orbits with along-track perturbations over one hundred kilometers. Twelve other satellites should show effects over one kilometer. Tracking them over their resonant beat periods could reveal valuable detail about Earth's high-order gravity field. Those details refine orbit prediction for all satellites.
nasa-tm-19700026484-an-analysis-of-the-p:
The Manned Spacecraft Center in Houston issued this internal note on June 16, 1969. It analyzes what the Saturn 5 launch vehicle could still do if two engines failed. The study covers both the remaining performance and how the huge rocket would behave in flight with two of its first stage engines out.

Discussion splits into vehicle performance first, then vehicle dynamics case by case. The failure cases pair the center engine with one control engine, and two control engines in opposed positions. Other cases lose two neighboring control engines at once, or one after the other partway through the burn. Each pairing steers and steadies the rocket differently, so each earns its own treatment.
nasa-tm-19710018396-tesseral-resonance-o:
B. E. Lowrey wrote this NASA preprint, numbered X-554-71-198, on a surprise in the orbit of IMP-4, also called Explorer 34. The satellite flew a highly eccentric orbit, looping far from Earth and back. Its time of closest approach, perigee passage, was being shifted by a resonance with Earth's gravity field.

The abstract traces the shift to the third harmonic of the field, the part describing its lumpiness at that scale. The perturbation swings the perigee time by about nine minutes over a period of roughly two hundred forty days. Lowrey notes the resonance arose because the orbital period nearly matched a simple fraction of Earth's rotation period. He suggests the effect can test current values of those harmonics, and that other eccentric orbits should show it too.
our-farm-of-four-acres-and-the-money-we-:
Miss Coulton's Our Farm of Four Acres tells how two women took a tiny farm and made it pay. By this 1860 printing the little book had reached its twelfth London edition. The preface answers critics in detail: yes, the first cow's legs were strapped, and she knocked man and pail down with her side anyway, until her calf was parted with. The landlord, by agreement, kept gates and buildings in repair; a stream, not hedges, bounds the meadows.

The women churned butter four hours at a time, turn and turn about, until practice cut the work to three quarters of an hour. Nearly eighteen months on, they report themselves as satisfied as ever with their profits. Pitied for never resting, they quote Poor Richard: leisure is the time for doing something useful. It is a founding text of back-to-the-land self-sufficiency.
pareto-manuale-economia-politica-1919-it:
Pareto restated his economics compactly in the Manuale di economia politica, here in its 1919 Italian printing. The manual gives his mature theory in short compass. Ophelimity, his coinage for the satisfaction a good gives, replaces the looser term utility. Indifference curves map how a buyer trades one good against another.

From those curves he builds toward the Pareto optimum, the best balance his system allows. The Italian text stands as a documentary original, since no public domain English translation exists. Students use the manual as the clearest door into his economics. Its appendix on math drew praise and complaint alike. The compact force is pure Pareto.
